entries.05d980fe9ad3c56fba3615445ce3714d64ce9138: <div sID="gen23679" type="x-p"/> <chapter n="25" osisID="Matt.25" sID="Matt.25"/> <div eID="gen23679" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23680" type="introduction"/> <div sID="gen23681" type="x-p"/> This chapter continues and concludes our Saviour's discourse, which began in the foregoing chapter, concerning his second coming and the end of the world. This was his farewell sermon of caution, as that, <reference osisRef="John.14.15-John.14.16">John xiv. 15, 16</reference>, was of comfort to his disciples; and they had need of both in a world of so much temptation and trouble as this is. The application of that discourse, was, Watch therefore, and be ye also ready. Now, in prosecution of these serious awakening cautions, in this chapter we have three parables, the scope of which is the same—to quicken us all with the utmost care and diligence to get ready for Christ's second coming, which, in all his farewells to his church, mention was made of, as in that before he died (<reference osisRef="John.14.2">John xiv. 2</reference>), in that at his ascension (<reference osisRef="Acts.1.11">Acts i. 11</reference>), and in that at the shutting up of the canon of the scriptures, <reference osisRef="Rev.22.20">Rev. xxii. 20</reference>. Now it concerns us to prepare for Christ's coming; I. That we may then be ready to attend upon him; and this is shown in the parable of the ten virgins, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.1-Matt.25.13">ver. 1-13</reference>. II. That we may then be ready to give u our account to him; and this is shown in the parable of the three servants, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.14-Matt.25.30">ver. 14-30</reference>. III. That we may then be ready to receive from him our final sentence, and that it may be to eternal life; and this is shown in a more plain description of the process of the last judgment, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.31-Matt.25.46">ver. 31-46</reference>. These are things of awful consideration, because of everlasting concern to every one of us.
entries.73a81f8e3ec650c19554b2fbe971724b130db5a6: <div eID="gen23681" type="x-p"/> <div eID="gen23680" type="introduction"/> <title type="x-s3">The Parable of the Ten Virgins.</title> <div sID="gen23682" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">1</hi> Then shall the kingdom of heaven be likened unto ten virgins, which took their lamps, and went forth to meet the bridegroom. <hi type="super">2</hi> And five of them were wise, and five <hi type="italic">were</hi> foolish. <hi type="super">3</hi> They that <hi type="italic">were</hi> foolish took their lamps, and took no oil with them: <hi type="super">4</hi> But the wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps. <hi type="super">5</hi> While the bridegroom tarried, they all slumbered and slept. <hi type="super">6</hi> And at midnight there was a cry made, Behold, the bridegroom cometh; go ye out to meet him. <hi type="super">7</hi> Then all those virgins arose, and trimmed their lamps. <hi type="super">8</hi> And the foolish said unto the wise, Give us of your oil; for our lamps are gone out. <hi type="super">9</hi> But the wise answered, saying, <hi type="italic">Not so;</hi> lest there be not enough for us and you: but go ye rather to them that sell, and buy for yourselves. <hi type="super">10</hi> And while they went to buy, the bridegroom came; and they that were ready went in with him to the marriage: and the door was shut. <hi type="super">11</hi> Afterward came also the other virgins, saying, Lord, Lord, open to us. <hi type="super">12</hi> But he answered and said, Verily I say unto you, I know you not. <hi type="super">13</hi> Watch therefore, for ye know neither the day nor the hour wherein the Son of man cometh. <div eID="gen23682" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23683" type="x-p"/> Here, <div eID="gen23683" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23684" type="x-p"/> I. That in general which is to be illustrated is, <hi type="italic">the kingdom of heaven,</hi> the state of things under the gospel, the external kingdom of Christ, and the administration and success of it. Some of Christ's parables had shown us what it is like now in the present reception of it, as <reference osisRef="Matt.13.1-Matt.13.52">ch. xiii.</reference> This tells us what it shall be like, when the mystery of God shall be finished, and that kingdom delivered up to the Father. The administration of Christ's government, towards the ready and the unready in the great day, may be illustrated by this similitude; or the kingdom is put for the subjects of the kingdom. The professors of Christianity shall then be likened to these ten virgins, and shall be thus distinguished. <div eID="gen23684" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23685" type="x-p"/> II. That by which it is illustrated, is, a marriage solemnity. It was a custom sometimes used among the Jews on that occasion, that the bridegroom came, attended with his friends, late in the night, to the house of the bride, where she expected him, attended with her bride-maids; who, upon notice given of the bridegrooms' approach, were to go out with lamps in their hands, to light him into the house with ceremony and formality, in order to the celebrating of the nuptials with great mirth. And some think that on these occasions they had usually <hi type="italic">ten virgins;</hi> for the Jews never held a synagogue, circumcised, kept the passover, or contracted marriage, but ten persons at least were present. Boaz, when he married Ruth, had <hi type="italic">ten witnesses,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ruth.4.2">Ruth iv. 2</reference>. Now in this parable, <div eID="gen23685" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23686" type="x-p"/> 1. The <hi type="italic">Bridegroom</hi> is our Lord Jesus Christ; he is so represented in the <reference osisRef="Ps.45.1-Ps.45.17">45th Psalm</reference>, 1, and often in the New Testament. It bespeaks his singular and superlative love to, and his faithful and inviolable covenant with, his spouse the church. Believers are now betrothed to Christ (<reference osisRef="Hos.2.19">Hos. ii. 19</reference>); but the solemnizing of the marriage is reserved for the great day, when the bride, the Lamb's wife, will have made herself completely ready, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.7">Rev. xix. 7</reference>, <reference osisRef="Rev.19.9">9</reference>. <div eID="gen23686" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23687" type="x-p"/> 2. The virgins are the professors of religion, members of the church; but here represented as <hi type="italic">her companions</hi> (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.14">Ps. xlv. 14</reference>), as elsewhere her <hi type="italic">children</hi> (<reference osisRef="Isa.54.1">Isa. liv. 1</reference>), her <hi type="italic">ornaments,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.49.18">Isa. xlix. 18</reference>. They that follow the Lamb, are said to be <hi type="italic">virgins</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.14.4">Rev. xiv. 4</reference>); this denotes their beauty and purity; they are to be presented as chaste <hi type="italic">virgins to Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.11.2">2 Cor. xi. 2</reference>. The bridegroom is a king; so these virgins are <hi type="italic">maids of honour,</hi> virgins <hi type="italic">without number</hi> (<reference osisRef="Song.6.8">Cant. vi. 8</reference>), yet here said to be <hi type="italic">ten.</hi> <div eID="gen23687" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23688" type="x-p"/> 3. The office of these virgins is to meet the bridegroom, which is as much their happiness as their duty. They come to wait <hi type="italic">upon</hi> the bridegroom when he appears, and in the mean time to wait <hi type="italic">for</hi> him. See here the nature of Christianity. As Christians, we profess ourselves to be, (1.) Attendants upon Christ, to do him honour, as the glorious Bridegroom, to be to him for a name and a praise, especially then when he shall come to be glorified in his saints. We must follow him as honorary servants do their masters, <reference osisRef="John.12.26">John xii. 26</reference>. Hold up the name, and hold forth the praise of the exalted Jesus; this is our business. (2.) Expectants of Christ, and of his second coming. As Christians, we profess, not only to believe and look for, but to love and long for, the appearing of Christ, and to act in our whole conversation with a regard to it. The second coming of Christ is the centre in which all the lines of our religion meet, and to which the whole of the divine life hath a constant reference and tendency. <div eID="gen23688" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23689" type="x-p"/> 4. Their chief concern is to have lights in their hands, when they attend the bridegroom, thus to do him honour and do him service. Note, Christians are children of light. The gospel is light, and they who receive it must not only be enlightened by it themselves, but must <hi type="italic">shine as lights,</hi> must <hi type="italic">hold it forth,</hi> <reference osisRef="Phil.2.15-Phil.2.16">Phil. ii. 15, 16</reference>. This in general. <div eID="gen23689" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23690" type="x-p"/> Now concerning these ten virgins, we may observe, <div eID="gen23690" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23691" type="x-p"/> (1.) Their different character, with the proof and evidence of it. <div eID="gen23691" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23692" type="x-p"/> [1.] Their character was that <hi type="italic">five were wise, and five foolish</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.2">v. 2</reference>); and <hi type="italic">wisdom excelleth folly, as far as light excelleth darkness;</hi> so saith Solomon, a competent judge, <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.13">Eccl. ii. 13</reference>. Note, Those of the same profession and denomination among men, may yet be of characters vastly different in the sight of God. Sincere Christians are the <hi type="italic">wise</hi> virgins, and hypocrites the <hi type="italic">foolish ones,</hi> as in another parable they are represented by wise and foolish builders. Note, Those are wise or foolish indeed, that are so in the affairs of their souls. True religion is true wisdom; sin is folly, but especially the sin of hypocrisy, for those are the greatest fools, that are <hi type="italic">wise in their own conceit,</hi> and those the worst of sinners, that <hi type="italic">feign themselves just men.</hi> Some observe from the equal number of the wise and foolish, what a charitable decorum (it is Archbishop Tillotson's expression) Christ observes, as if he would hope that the number of true believers was nearly equal to that of hypocrites, or, at least, would teach us to hope the best concerning those that profess religion, and to think of them with a bias to the charitable side. Though, in judging of ourselves, we ought to remember that the gate is strait, and few find it; yet, in judging of others, we ought to remember that the Captain of our salvation brings many sons to glory. <div eID="gen23692" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23693" type="x-p"/> [2.] The evidence of this character was in the very thing which they were to attend to; by that they are judged of. <div eID="gen23693" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23694" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> It was the folly of the foolish virgins, that they <hi type="italic">took their lamps, and took no oil with them,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.25.3">v. 3</reference>. They had just the oil enough to make their lamps burn for the present, to make a show with, as if they intended to meet the bridegroom; but no cruse or bottle of oil with them for a recruit if the bridegroom tarried; thus hypocrites, <div eID="gen23694" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23695" type="x-p"/> 1. They have no principle within. They have a lamp of profession in their hands, but have not in their hearts that stock of sound knowledge, rooted dispositions, and settled resolutions, which is necessary to carry them through the services and trials of the present state. They act under the influence of external inducements, but are void of spiritual life; like a tradesman, that sets up without a stock, or the seed on the stony ground, that wanted root. <div eID="gen23695" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23696" type="x-p"/> 2. They have no prospect of, nor make provision for, what is to come. They took lamps for a present show, but not oil for after use. This incogitancy is the ruin of many professors; all their care is to recommend themselves to their neighbours, whom they now converse with, not to approve themselves to Christ, whom they must hereafter appear before; as if any thing will serve, provide it will but serve for the present. Tell them of things not seen as yet, and you are like Lot to his sons-in-law, as one that mocked. They do not provide for hereafter, as the ant does, nor <hi type="italic">lay up for the time to come,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.19">1 Tim. vi. 19</reference>. <div eID="gen23696" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23697" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> It was the wisdom of the wise virgins, that <hi type="italic">they took oil in their vessels with their lamps,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.25.4">v. 4</reference>. They had a good principle within, which would maintain and keep up their profession. 1. The heart is the vessel, which it is our wisdom to get furnished; for, out of a good treasure there, good things must be brought; but if that root be rottenness, the blossom will be dust. 2. Grace is the <hi type="italic">oil</hi> which we must have in this <hi type="italic">vessel;</hi> in the tabernacle there was constant provision made of <hi type="italic">oil for the light,</hi> <reference osisRef="Exod.35.14">Exod. xxxv. 14</reference>. Our light must shine before men in good works, but this cannot be, or not long, unless there be a fixed active principle in the heart, of faith in Christ, and love to God and our brethren, from which we must act in every thing we do in religion, with an eye to what is before us. They that took oil in their vessels, did it upon supposition that perhaps the bridegroom might tarry. Note, In looking forward it is good to prepare for the worst, to lay in for a long siege. But remember that this oil which keeps the lamps burning, is derived to the candlestick from Jesus Christ, the great and good <hi type="italic">Olive,</hi> by the <hi type="italic">golden pipes</hi> of the ordinances, as it is represented in that vision (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.2-Zech.4.3">Zech. iv. 2, 3</reference>, <reference osisRef="Zech.4.12">12</reference>), which is explained <reference osisRef="John.1.16">John i. 16</reference>, <hi type="italic">Of his fulness have all we received, and grace for grace.</hi> <div eID="gen23697" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23698" type="x-p"/> (2.) Their common fault, during the bridegroom's delay; <hi type="italic">They all slumbered and slept,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.25.5">v. 5</reference>. Observe here, <div eID="gen23698" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23699" type="x-p"/> [1.] The bridegroom tarried, that is, he did not come out so soon as they expected. What we look for as certain, we are apt to think is very near; many in the apostles' times imagined that the <hi type="italic">day of the Lord was at hand,</hi> but it is not so. Christ, as to us, <hi type="italic">seems</hi> to tarry, and yet really <hi type="italic">does not,</hi> <reference osisRef="Hab.2.3">Hab. ii. 3</reference>. There is good reason for the Bridegroom's tarrying; there are many intermediate counsels and purposes to be accomplished, the elect must all be called in, God's patience must be manifested, and the saints' patience tried, the harvest of the earth must be ripened, and so must the harvest of heaven too. But though Christ tarry past <hi type="italic">our</hi> time, he will not tarry past the <hi type="italic">due</hi> time. <div eID="gen23699" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23700" type="x-p"/> [2.] While he tarried, those that waited for him, grew careless, and forgot what they were attending; <hi type="italic">They all slumbered and slept;</hi> as if they had given over looking for him; for <hi type="italic">when the Son of man cometh,</hi> he will <hi type="italic">not find faith,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.18.8">Luke xviii. 8</reference>. Those that inferred the suddenness of it from its certainty, when that answered not their expectation, were apt from the delay to infer its uncertainty. The wise virgins slumbered, and the foolish slept; so some distinguish it; however, they were both faulty. The wise virgins kept their lamps burning, but did not keep themselves awake. Note, Too many good Christians, when they have been long in profession, grow remiss in their preparations for Christ's second coming; they intermit their care, abate their zeal, their graces are not lively, nor their works found perfect before God; and though all <hi type="italic">love</hi> be not lost, yet the <hi type="italic">first</hi> love is left. If it was hard to the disciples to watch with Christ <hi type="italic">an hour,</hi> much more to watch with him <hi type="italic">an age. I sleep,</hi> saith the spouse, <hi type="italic">but my heart wakes,</hi> Observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> They slumbered, and then they slept. Note, One degree of carelessness and remissness makes way for another. Those that allow themselves in slumbering, will scarcely keep themselves from sleeping; therefore dread the beginning of spiritual decays; <hi type="italic">Venienti occurrite morbo—Attend to the first symptoms of disease.</hi> The ancients generally understood the virgins' slumbering and sleeping of their dying; they all died, wise and foolish (<reference osisRef="Ps.49.10">Ps. xlix. 10</reference>), before judgment-day. So Ferus, <hi type="italic">Antequam veniat sponsus omnibus obdormiscendum est, hoc est, moriendum—Before the Bridegroom come, all must sleep, that is, die.</hi> So Calvin. But I think it is rather to be taken as we have opened it. <div eID="gen23700" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23701" type="x-p"/> (3.) The surprising summons given them, to attend the bridegroom (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.6">v. 6</reference>); <hi type="italic">At midnight there was a cry made, Behold, the bridegroom cometh.</hi> Note, [1.] Though Christ tarry long, he will come at last; though he seem slow, he is sure. In his first coming, he was thought long by those that waited for the consolation of Israel; yet in the <hi type="italic">fulness of time</hi> he came; so his second coming, though long deferred, is not forgotten; his enemies shall find, to their cost, that forbearance is no acquittance; and his friends shall find, to their comfort, that <hi type="italic">the vision is for an appointed time, and at the end it shall speak, and not lie.</hi> The year of the redeemed is fixed, and it will come. [2.] Christ's coming will be at our midnight, when we least look for him, and are most disposed to take our rest. His coming for the relief and comfort of his people, often is when the good intended seems to be at the greatest distance; and his coming to reckon with his enemies, is when they put the evil day furthest from them. It was at midnight that the first-born of Egypt were destroyed, and Israel delivered, <reference osisRef="Exod.12.29">Exod. xii. 29</reference>. Death often comes when it is least expected; the soul is <hi type="italic">required this night,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.12.20">Luke xii. 20</reference>. Christ will come when he pleases, to show his sovereignty, and will not let us know when, to teach us our duty. [3.] When Christ comes, we must <hi type="italic">go forth to meet him.</hi> As Christians we are bound to attend all the motions of the Lord Jesus, and meet him in all his out-goings. When he comes to us at death, we must go forth out of the body, out of the world, to meet him with affections and workings of soul suitable to the discoveries we then expect him to make of himself. <hi type="italic">Go ye forth to meet him,</hi> is a call to those who are habitually prepared, to be actually ready. [4.] The notice given of Christ's approach, and the call to meet him, will be awakening; <hi type="italic">There was a cry made.</hi> His first coming was not with any observation at all, nor did they say, <hi type="italic">Lo, here is Christ,</hi> or <hi type="italic">Lo, he is there; he was in the world, and the world knew him not;</hi> but his second coming will be with the observation of all the world; <hi type="italic">Every eye shall see him.</hi> There will be a cry from heaven, for he shall <hi type="italic">descend with a shout, Arise, ye dead, and come to judgment;</hi> and a cry from the earth too, a <hi type="italic">cry to rocks and mountains,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.6.16">Rev. vi. 16</reference>. <div eID="gen23701" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23702" type="x-p"/> (4.) The address they all made to answer this summons (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.7">v. 7</reference>); <hi type="italic">They all arose, and trimmed their lamps,</hi> snuffed them and supplied them with oil and went about with all expedition to put themselves in a posture to receive the bridegroom. Now, [1.] This, in the wise virgins, bespeaks an actual preparation for the Bridegroom's coming. Note, even those that are best prepared for death, have, upon the immediate arrests of it, work to do, to get themselves actually ready, that they may be <hi type="italic">found in peace</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.14">2 Pet. iii. 14</reference>), <hi type="italic">found doing</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.46">ch. xxiv. 46</reference>), and not <hi type="italic">found naked,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.3">2 Cor. v. 3</reference>. It will be a day of search and enquiry; and it concerns us to think how we shall then be found. When we see the day approaching, we must address ourselves to our dying work with all seriousness, renewing our repentance for sin, our consent to the covenant, our farewells to the world; and our souls must be carried out toward God in suitable breathings. [2.] In the foolish virgins, it denotes a vain confidence, and conceit of the goodness of their state, and their readiness for another world. Note, Even counterfeit graces will serve a man to make a show of when he comes to die, as well as they have done all his life long; the hypocrite's hopes blaze when they are just expiring, like a lightening before death. <div eID="gen23702" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23703" type="x-p"/> (5.) The distress which the foolish virgins were in, for want of <hi type="italic">oil,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.25.8-Matt.25.9">v. 8, 9</reference>. This bespeaks, [1.] The apprehensions which some hypocrites have of the misery of their state, even on this side death, when God opens their eyes to see their folly, and themselves perishing <hi type="italic">with a lie in their right hand.</hi> Or, however, [2.] The real misery of their state on the other side death, and in the judgment; how far their fair, but false, profession of religion will be from availing them any thing in the great day; see what comes of it. <div eID="gen23703" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23704" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Their lamps are gone out. The lamps of hypocrites often go out in this life; when they who have begun in the spirit, end in the flesh, and the hypocrisy breaks out in an open apostasy, <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.20">2 Pet. ii. 20</reference>. The profession withers, and the credit of it is lost; the hopes fail, and the comfort of them is gone; how often is <hi type="italic">the candle of the wicked</hi> thus <hi type="italic">put out?</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.21.17">Job xxi. 17</reference>. Yet many a hypocrite keeps up his credit, and the comfort of his profession, such as it is, to the last; but what is it when <hi type="italic">God taketh away his soul?</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.27.8">Job xxvii. 8</reference>. If his candle be not put out <hi type="italic">before</hi> him, it is put out <hi type="italic">with him,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.18.5-Job.18.6">Job xviii. 5, 6</reference>. He shall <hi type="italic">lie down in sorrow,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.50.11">Isa. l. 11</reference>. The gains of a hypocritical profession will not follow a man to judgment, <reference osisRef="Matt.7.22-Matt.7.23">ch. vii. 22, 23</reference>. The lamps are gone out, when the hypocrite's hope proves <hi type="italic">like the spider's web</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.8.11">Job viii. 11</reference>, &c.), and like the <hi type="italic">giving up of the ghost</hi> (<reference osisRef="Job.11.20">Job xi. 20</reference>), like Absalom's mule that left him in the oak. <div eID="gen23704" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23705" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They wanted oil to supply them when they were going out. Note, Those that take up short of true grace, will certainly find the want of it one time or other. An external profession well humoured may carry a man far, but it will not carry him through; it may light him along this world, but the damps of the valley of the shadow of death will put it out. <div eID="gen23705" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23706" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> They would gladly be beholden to the wise virgins for a supply out of their vessels; <hi type="italic">Give us of your oil.</hi> Note, The day is coming, when carnal hypocrites would gladly be found in the condition of true Christians. Those who now hate the strictness of religion, will, at death and judgment, wish for the solid comforts of it. Those who care not to live the life, yet would die the death, of the righteous. The day is coming when those who now look with contempt upon humble contrite saints, would gladly get an interest in them, and would value those as their best friends and benefactors, whom now they <hi type="italic">set with the dogs of their flock. Give us of your oil;</hi> that is, "Speak a good word for us;" so some; but there is no occasion for vouchers in the great day, the Judge knows what is every man's true character. But is it not well that they are brought to say, <hi type="italic">Give us of your oil?</hi> It is so; but, 1. This request was extorted by sensible necessity. Note, Those will see their need of grace hereafter, when it should save them, who will not see their need of grace now, when it should sanctify and rule them. (2.) It comes too late. God would have given them oil, had they asked in time; but there is no buying when the market is over, no bidding when the inch of candle is dropped. <div eID="gen23706" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23707" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Fourthly,</hi> They were denied a share in their companions' oil. It is a sad presage of a repulse with God, when they were thus repulsed by good people. <hi type="italic">The wise answered, Not so;</hi> that peremptory denial is not in the original, but supplied by the translators: these wise virgins would rather give a reason without a positive refusal, than (as many do) give a positive refusal without a reason. They were well inclined to help their neighbours in distress; but, We must not, we cannot, we dare not, do it, <hi type="italic">lest there be not enough for us and you;</hi> charity begins at home; but <hi type="italic">go, and buy for yourselves.</hi> Note, 1. Those that would be saved, must have grace of their own. Though we have benefit by the communion of saints, and the faith and prayers of others may now redound to our advantage, yet our own sanctification is indispensably necessary to our own salvation. The just shall live by his faith. Every man shall give account of himself, and therefore let every man <hi type="italic">prove his own work;</hi> for he cannot get another to muster for him in that day. 2. Those that have most grace, have none to spare; all we have, is little enough for ourselves to appear before God in. The best have need to borrow from Christ, but they have none to lend to any of their neighbours. The church of Rome, which dreams of works of supererogation and the imputation of the righteousness of saints, forgets that it was the wisdom of the wise virgins to understand that they had but oil enough for themselves, and none for others. But observe, These wise virgins do not upbraid the foolish with their neglect, nor boast of their own forecast, nor torment them with suggestions tending to despair, but give them the best advice the case will bear, <hi type="italic">Go ye rather to them that sell.</hi> Note, Those that deal foolishly in the affairs of their souls, are to be pitied, and not insulted over; for who made thee to differ? When ministers attend such as have been mindless of God and their souls all their days, but are under death-bed convictions; and, because true repentance is never too late, direct them to repent, and turn to God, and close with Christ; yet, because late repentance is seldom true, they do but as these wise virgins did by the foolish, even made the best of bad. They can but tell them what is to be done, if it be not too late, but whether the door may not be shut before it is done, is an unspeakable hazard. It is good advice now, if it be taken in time, <hi type="italic">Go to them that sell, and buy for yourselves.</hi> Note, Those that would have grace, must have recourse to, and attend upon, the means of grace. See <reference osisRef="Isa.55.1">Isa. lv. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen23707" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23708" type="x-p"/> (6.) The coming of the bridegroom, and the issue of all this different character of the wise and foolish virgins. See what came of it. <div eID="gen23708" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23709" type="x-p"/> [1.] <hi type="italic">While they went out to buy, the bridegroom came.</hi> Note, With regard to those that put off their great work to the last, it is a thousand to one, that they have not time to do it then. Getting grace is a work of time, and cannot be done in a hurry. While the poor awakened soul addresses itself, upon a sick bed, to repentance and prayer, in awful confusion, it scarcely knows which end to begin at, or what to do first; and presently death comes, judgment comes, and the work is undone, and the poor sinner undone for ever. This comes of having oil to buy when we should burn it, and grace to get when we should use it. <div eID="gen23709" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23710" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">The bridegroom came.</hi> Note, Our Lord Jesus will come to his people, at the great day, as a Bridegroom; will come in pomp and rich attire, attended with his friends: now that the Bridegroom is taken away from us, <hi type="italic">we fast</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.9.15">ch. ix. 15</reference>), but then will be an everlasting feast. Then the Bridegroom will fetch home his bride, to be <hi type="italic">where he is</hi> (<reference osisRef="John.17.24">John xvii. 24</reference>), and will <hi type="italic">rejoice over his bride,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.62.5">Isa. lii. 5</reference>. <div eID="gen23710" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23711" type="x-p"/> [2.] <hi type="italic">They that were ready, went in with him to the marriage.</hi> Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> To be eternally glorified is to go in with Christ to the marriage, to be in his immediate presence, and in the most intimate fellowship and communion with him in a state of eternal rest, joy, and plenty. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Those, and those only, shall go to heaven hereafter, that are made ready for heaven here, that are <hi type="italic">wrought to the self-same thing,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.5.5">2 Cor. v. 5</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> The suddenness of death, and of Christ's coming to us then, will be no obstruction to our happiness, if we have been habitually prepared. <div eID="gen23711" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23712" type="x-p"/> [3.] <hi type="italic">The door was shut,</hi> as is usual when all the company is come, that are to be admitted. The door was shut, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> To secure those that were within; that, being now made <hi type="italic">pillars in the house of our God, they may go no more out,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.3.12">Rev. iii. 12</reference>. Adam was put into paradise, but the door was left open and so he went out again; but when glorified saints are put into the heavenly paradise, they are shut in. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> To exclude those that were out. The state of saints and sinners will then be unalterably fixed, and those that are shut out then, will be shut out for ever. Now the gate is strait, yet it is open; but then it will be shut and bolted, and <hi type="italic">a great gulf fixed.</hi> This was like the shutting of the door of the ark when Noah was in; as he was thereby preserved, so all the rest were finally abandoned. <div eID="gen23712" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23713" type="x-p"/> [4.] The foolish virgins came when it was <hi type="italic">too late</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.11">v. 11</reference>); <hi type="italic">Afterward came also the other virgins.</hi> Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> There are many that will seek admission into heaven when it is too late; as profane Esau, who <hi type="italic">afterward would have inherited the blessing.</hi> God and religion will be glorified by those late solicitations, though sinners will not be saved by them; it is for the honour of <hi type="italic">Lord, Lord,</hi> that, of fervent and importunate prayer, that those who slight it now, will flee to it shortly, and it will not be called whining and canting then. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The vain confidence of hypocrites will carry them very far in their expectations of happiness. They go to heaven-gate, and demand entrance, and yet are shut out; lifted up to heaven in a fond conceit of the goodness of their state, and yet thrust down to hell. <div eID="gen23713" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23714" type="x-p"/> [5.] They were <hi type="italic">rejected,</hi> as Esau was (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.12">v. 12</reference>); <hi type="italic">I know you not.</hi> Note, We are all concerned to <hi type="italic">seek the Lord while he may be found;</hi> for there is a time coming when he will not be found. Time was, when, <hi type="italic">Lord, Lord, open to us,</hi> would have sped well, by virtue of that promise, <hi type="italic">Knock, and it shall be opened to you;</hi> but now it comes too late. The sentence is solemnly bound on with, <hi type="italic">Verily I say unto you,</hi> which amounts to no less than <hi type="italic">swearing in his wrath, that they shall never enter into his rest.</hi> It bespeaks him resolved, and them silenced by it. <div eID="gen23714" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23715" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> Here is a practical inference drawn from this parable (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.13">v. 13</reference>); <hi type="italic">Watch therefore,</hi> We had it before (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.42">ch. xxiv. 42</reference>), and here it is repeated as the most needful caution. Note, 1. Our great duty is to watch, to attend to the business of our souls with the utmost diligence and circumspection. Be awake, and be wakeful. 2. It is a good reason for our watching, that the time of our Lord's coming is very uncertain; <hi type="italic">we know neither the day nor the hour.</hi> Therefore every day and every hour we must be ready, and not off our watch any day in the year, or any hour in the day. Be thou <hi type="italic">in the fear of the Lord</hi> every day and <hi type="italic">all the day long.</hi>
entries.f0aa62ce142bdfe1b72f3a06dff3e61193199c44: <div eID="gen23715" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Parable of the Talents.</title> <div sID="gen23716" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">14</hi> For <hi type="italic">the kingdom of heaven is</hi> as a man travelling into a far country, <hi type="italic">who</hi> called his own servants, and delivered unto them his goods. <hi type="super">15</hi> And unto one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one; to every man according to his several ability; and straightway took his journey. 16 Then he that had received the five talents went and traded with the same, and made <hi type="italic">them</hi> other five talents. 17 And likewise he that <hi type="italic">had received</hi> two, he also gained other two. <hi type="super">18</hi> But he that had received one went and digged in the earth, and hid his lord's money. <hi type="super">19</hi> After a long time the lord of those servants cometh, and reckoneth with them. <hi type="super">20</hi> And so he that had received five talents came and brought other five talents, saying, Lord, thou deliveredst unto me five talents: behold, I have gained beside them five talents more. 21 His lord said unto him, Well done, <hi type="italic">thou</hi> good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord. <hi type="super">22</hi> He also that had received two talents came and said, Lord, thou deliveredst unto me two talents: behold, I have gained two other talents beside them. <hi type="super">23</hi> His lord said unto him, Well done, good and faithful servant; thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things: enter thou into the joy of thy lord. <hi type="super">24</hi> Then he which had received the one talent came and said, Lord, I knew thee that thou art a hard man, reaping where thou hast not sown, and gathering where thou hast not strawed: <hi type="super">25</hi> And I was afraid, and went and hid thy talent in the earth: lo, <hi type="italic">there</hi> thou hast <hi type="italic">that is</hi> thine. <hi type="super">26</hi> His lord answered and said unto him, <hi type="italic">Thou</hi> wicked and slothful servant, thou knewest that I reap where I sowed not, and gather where I have not strawed: <hi type="super">27</hi> Thou oughtest therefore to have put my money to the exchangers, and <hi type="italic">then</hi> at my coming I should have received mine own with usury. <hi type="super">28</hi> Take therefore the talent from him, and give <hi type="italic">it</hi> unto him which hath ten talents. <hi type="super">29</hi> For unto every one that hath shall be given, and he shall have abundance: but from him that hath not shall be taken away even that which he hath. <hi type="super">30</hi> And cast ye the unprofitable servant into outer darkness: there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth. <div eID="gen23716" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23717" type="x-p"/> We have here the parable of the <hi type="italic">talents</hi> committed to three servants; this implies that we are in a state of work and business, as the former implies that we are in a state of expectancy. <hi type="italic">That</hi> showed the necessity of habitual preparation, <hi type="italic">this</hi> of actual diligence in our present work and service. In <hi type="italic">that</hi> we were stirred up to do well for our own souls; in <hi type="italic">this</hi> to lay out ourselves for the glory of God and the good of others. <div eID="gen23717" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23718" type="x-p"/> In this parable, 1. The <hi type="italic">Master</hi> is Christ, who is the absolute Owner and Proprietor of all persons and things, and in a special manner of his church; into his hands all things are delivered. 2. The <hi type="italic">servants</hi> are Christians, his own servants, so they are called; born in his house, bought with his money, devoted to his praise, and employed in his work. It is probable that <hi type="italic">ministers</hi> are specially intended here, who are more immediately attending on him, and sent by him. St. Paul often calls himself a <hi type="italic">servant of Jesus Christ.</hi> See <reference osisRef="2Tim.2.24">2 Tim. ii. 24</reference>. <div eID="gen23718" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23719" type="x-p"/> We have three things, in general, in this parable. <div eID="gen23719" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23720" type="x-p"/> I. The trust committed to these servants; Their master <hi type="italic">delivered to them his goods:</hi> having appointed them to work (for Christ keeps no servants to be idle), he left them something to work upon. Note, 1. Christ's servants have and receive their all from him; for they are of themselves worth nothing, nor have any thing they can call their own but sin. 2. Our receiving from Christ is in order to our working for him. Our privileges are intended to find us with business. The <hi type="italic">manifestation of the Spirit</hi> is given to every man to <hi type="italic">profit withal.</hi> 3. Whatever we receive to be made use of for Christ, still the property is vested in him; we are but tenants upon his land, <hi type="italic">stewards of his manifold grace,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.4.10">1 Pet. iv. 10</reference>. Now observe here, <div eID="gen23720" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23721" type="x-p"/> (1.) On what occasion this trust was committed to these servants: The master was <hi type="italic">travelling into a far country.</hi> This is explained, <reference osisRef="Eph.4.8">Eph. iv. 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">When he ascended on high, he gave gifts to men.</hi> Note, [1.] When Christ went to heaven, he was as a man <hi type="italic">travelling into a far country;</hi> that is, he went with a purpose to be away a great while. [2.] When he went, he took care to furnish his church with all things necessary for it during his personal absence. For, and in consideration of, his departure, he committed to his church truths, laws, promises and powers; these were the <hi type="bold"><hi type="italic">parakatatheke</hi></hi>—<hi type="italic">the great depositum</hi> (as it is called, <reference osisRef="1Tim.6.20">1 Tim. vi. 20</reference>; <reference osisRef="2Tim.1.14">2 Tim. i. 14</reference>), the <hi type="italic">good thing</hi> that is committed to us; and he sent his Spirit to enable his servants to teach and profess those truths, to press and observe those laws, to improve and apply those promises, and to exercise and employ those powers, ordinary or extraordinary. Thus Christ, at his ascension, left his goods to his church. <div eID="gen23721" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23722" type="x-p"/> (2.) In what proportion this trust was committed. [1.] He gave <hi type="italic">talents;</hi> a talent of silver is computed to be in our money three hundred and fifty-three pounds eleven shillings and ten pence halfpenny; so the learned Bishop Cumberland. Note, Christ's gifts are rich and valuable, the purchases of his blood inestimable, and none of them mean. [2.] He gave to some more, to others less; to one <hi type="italic">five</hi> talents, to another <hi type="italic">two,</hi> to another <hi type="italic">one;</hi> to every one according to his several ability. When Divine Providence has made a difference in men's ability, as to mind, body, estate, relation, and interest, divine grace dispenses spiritual gifts accordingly, but still the ability itself is from him. Observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Every one had some one talent at least, and that is not a despicable stock for a poor servant to begin with. A <hi type="italic">soul</hi> of our own is the <hi type="italic">one</hi> talent we are every one of us entrusted with, and it will find us with work. <hi type="italic">Hoc nempe ab homine exigiture, ut prosit hominibus; si fieri potest, multis; si minus, paucis; si minus, proximis, si minus, sibi: nam cum se utilem cæteris efficit, commune agit negotium. Et si quis bene de se meretur, hoc ipso aliis prodest quod aliis profuturum parat—It is the duty of a man to render himself beneficial to those around him; to a great number if possible; but if this is denied him, to a few; to his intimate connections; or, at least, to himself. He that is useful to others, may be reckoned a common good. And whoever entitles himself to his own approbation, is serviceable to others, as forming himself to those habits which will result in their favour.</hi> Seneca de Otio Sapient. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> All had not alike, for they had not all alike abilities and opportunities. God is a free Agent, <hi type="italic">dividing to every man severally as he will;</hi> some are cut out for service in one kind, others in another, as the members of the natural body. When the householder had thus settled his affairs, he <hi type="italic">straightway took his journey.</hi> Our Lord Jesus, when he had given commandments to his apostles, as one in haste to be gone, went to heaven. <div eID="gen23722" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23723" type="x-p"/> II. The different management and improvement of this trust, which we have an account of, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.16-Matt.25.18">v. 16-18</reference>. <div eID="gen23723" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23724" type="x-p"/> 1. Two of the servants did well. <div eID="gen23724" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23725" type="x-p"/> (1.) They were diligent and faithful; <hi type="italic">They went, and traded;</hi> they put the money they were entrusted with, to the use for which it was intended—laid it out in goods, and made returns of it; as soon as ever their master was gone, they immediately applied themselves to their business. Those that have so much work to do, as every Christian has, need to set about it quickly, and lose not time. <hi type="italic">They went, and traded.</hi> Note, A true Christian is a spiritual tradesman. Trades are called <hi type="italic">mysteries,</hi> and <hi type="italic">without controversy great is the mystery of godliness;</hi> it is a manufacture trade; there is something to be done by upon our own hearts, and for the good of others. It is a merchant-trade; things of less value to us are parted with for things of greater value; <hi type="italic">wisdom's merchandize,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.3.15">Prov. iii. 15</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.13.45">Matt. xiii. 45</reference>. A tradesman is one who, having made his trade his choice, and taken pains to learn it, makes it his business to follow it, lays out all he has for the advancement of it, makes all other affairs bend to it, and lives upon the gain of it. Thus does a true Christian act in the work of religion; we have no stock of our <hi type="italic">own</hi> to trade with, but trade as factors with our master's stock. The endowments of the mind—reason, wit, learning, must be used in subserviency to religion; the enjoyments of the world—estate, credit, interest, power, preferment, must be improved for the honour of Christ. The ordinances of the gospel, and our opportunities of attending them, bibles, ministers, sabbaths, sacraments, must be improved for the end for which they were instituted, and communion with God kept up by them, and the gifts and graces of the Spirit must be exercised; and this is trading with our talents. <div eID="gen23725" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23726" type="x-p"/> (2.) They were successful; they doubled their stock, and in a little time made <hi type="italic">cent. per cent.</hi> of it: he that had <hi type="italic">five talents,</hi> soon made them <hi type="italic">other five.</hi> Trading with our talents is not alway successful with others, but, however, it shall be so to ourselves, <reference osisRef="Isa.49.4">Isa. xlix. 4</reference>. Note, The hand of the diligent makes rich in graces, and comforts, and treasures of good works. There is a great deal to be got by industry in religion. <div eID="gen23726" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23727" type="x-p"/> Observe, The returns were in proportion to the receivings. [1.] From those to whom God hath given five talents, he expects the improvement of five, and to reap plentifully where he sows plentifully. The greater gifts any have, the more pains they ought to take, as those must that have a large stock to manage. [2.] From those to whom he has given but two talents, he expects only the improvement of two, which may encourage those who are placed in a lower and narrower sphere of usefulness; if they lay out themselves to do good according to the best of their capacity and opportunity, they shall be accepted, though they do not so much good as others. <div eID="gen23727" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23728" type="x-p"/> 2. The third did ill (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.18">v. 18</reference>); <hi type="italic">He that had received one talent, went, and hid his lord's money.</hi> Though the parable represents but one in three unfaithful, yet in a history that answers this <hi type="italic">parable,</hi> we find the disproportion quite the other way, when <hi type="italic">ten lepers were cleansed, nine</hi> of <hi type="italic">ten</hi> hid the talent, and <hi type="italic">only one returned to give thanks,</hi> <reference osisRef="Luke.17.17-Luke.17.18">Luke xvii. 17, 18</reference>. The unfaithful servant was he that had but <hi type="italic">one</hi> talent: doubtless there are many that have five talents, and bury them all; great abilities, great advantages, and yet do no good with them: but Christ would hint to us, (1.) That if he that had but one talent, be reckoned with thus for burying that one, much more will they be accounted offenders, that have more, that have many, and bury them. If he that was but of small capacity, was cast into utter darkness because he did not improve what he had as he might have done, <hi type="italic">of how much sorer punishment, suppose ye, shall he be thought worthy, that tramples underfoot the greatest advantages?</hi> (2.) That those who have least to do for God, frequently do least of what they have to do. Some make it an excuse for their laziness, that they have not the opportunities of serving God that others have; and because they have not wherewithal to do what they say they would, they will not do what we are sure they can, and so sit down and do nothing; it is really an aggravation of their sloth, that when they have but one talent to take care about, they neglect that one. <div eID="gen23728" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23729" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">He digged in the earth, and hid the talent,</hi> for fear it should be stolen; he did not misspend or misemploy it, did not embezzle it or squander it away, but he <hi type="italic">hid it.</hi> Money is like manure (so my Lord Bacon used to say,) good for nothing in the heap, but it must be spread; yet it is an evil which we have often seen under the sun, <hi type="italic">treasure heaped together</hi> (<reference osisRef="Jas.5.3">Jam. v. 3</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.6.1-Eccl.6.2">Eccl. vi. 1, 2</reference>), which does good to nobody; and so it is in spiritual gifts; many have them, and make no use of them for the end for which they were given them. Those that have estates, and do not lay them out in works of piety and charity; that have power and interest, and do not with it promote religion in the places where they live; ministers that have capacities and opportunities of doing good, but do not stir up the gift that is in them, are those slothful servants that seek their own things more than Christ's. <div eID="gen23729" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23730" type="x-p"/> He hid his <hi type="italic">lord's</hi> money; had it been his <hi type="italic">own,</hi> he might have done as he pleased; but, whatever abilities and advantages we have, they are not our <hi type="italic">own,</hi> we are but stewards of them, and must give account to our Lord, whose goods they are. It was an aggravation of his slothfulness, that his fellow-servants were busy and successful in trading, and their zeal should have provoked his. Are others active, and shall we be idle? <div eID="gen23730" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23731" type="x-p"/> III. The account of this improvement, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.19">v. 19</reference>. 1. The account is deferred; it is not <hi type="italic">till after a long time</hi> that they are reckoned with; not that the master neglects his affairs, or that God is <hi type="italic">slack concerning his promise</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Pet.3.9">2 Pet. iii. 9</reference>); no, he is <hi type="italic">ready to judge</hi> (<reference osisRef="1Pet.4.5">1 Pet. iv. 5</reference>); but every thing must be done in its time and order. 2. Yet the day of account comes at last; <hi type="italic">The lord of those servants reckoneth with them.</hi> Note, The stewards of the manifold grace of God must shortly <hi type="italic">give account of their stewardship.</hi> We must all be reckoned with—what good we have got to our own souls, and what good we have done to others by the advantages we have enjoyed. See <reference osisRef="Rom.14.10-Rom.14.11">Rom. xiv. 10, 11</reference>. Now here is, <div eID="gen23731" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23732" type="x-p"/> (1.) The good account of the faithful servants; and here observe, <div eID="gen23732" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23733" type="x-p"/> [1.] The servants <hi type="italic">giving up the account</hi> (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.20">v. 20</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.22">22</reference>); "<hi type="italic">Lord, thou deliveredst to me five talents,</hi> and to me <hi type="italic">two;</hi> behold, <hi type="italic">I have gained five talents,</hi> and I <hi type="italic">two</hi> talents <hi type="italic">more.</hi>" <div eID="gen23733" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23734" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Christ's faithful servants acknowledge with thankfulness his vouchsafements to them; <hi type="italic">Lord, thou deliveredst to me</hi> such and such things. Note, 1. It is good to keep a particular account of our receivings from God, to remember what we have received, that we may know what is expected from us, and may render according to the benefit. 2. We must never look upon our improvements but with a general mention of God's favour to us, of the honour he has put upon us, in entrusting us with his goods, and of that grace which is the spring and fountain of all the good that is in us or is done by us. For the truth is, the more we do for God, the more we are indebted to him for making use of us, and enabling us, for his service. <div eID="gen23734" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23735" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> They produce, as an evidence of their faithfulness, what they have gained. Note, God's good stewards have something to show for their diligence; <hi type="italic">Show me thy faith by thy works.</hi> He that is a good man, <hi type="italic">let him show it,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jas.3.13">Jam. iii. 13</reference>. If we be careful in our spiritual trade, it will soon be seen by us, and <hi type="italic">our works will follow us,</hi> <reference osisRef="Rev.14.13">Rev. xiv. 13</reference>. Not that the saints will in the great day make mention of their own good deeds; no, Christ will do that for them (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.35">v. 35</reference>); but it intimates that they who faithfully improve their talents, <hi type="italic">shall have boldness in the day of Christ,</hi> <reference osisRef="1John.2.28-1John.4.17">1 John ii. 28-iv. 17</reference>. And it is observable that he who had but <hi type="italic">two</hi> talents, gave up his account as cheerfully as he who had <hi type="italic">five;</hi> for our comfort, in the day of account, will be according to our faithfulness, not according to our usefulness; our sincerity, not our success; according to the uprightness of our hearts, not according to the degree of our opportunities. <div eID="gen23735" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23736" type="x-p"/> [2.] The master's acceptance and approbation of their account, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.21">v. 21</reference>, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.23">23</reference>. <div eID="gen23736" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23737" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> He commended them; <hi type="italic">Well done, good and faithful servant.</hi> Note, The diligence and integrity of those who approve themselves the good and faithful servants of Jesus Christ, will certainly be <hi type="italic">found to praise, and honour, and glory, at his appearing,</hi> <reference osisRef="1Pet.1.7">1 Pet. i. 7</reference>. Those that own and honour God now, he will own and honour shortly. 1. Their persons will be accepted; <hi type="italic">Thou good and faithful servant.</hi> He that knows the integrity of his servants now, will witness to it in the great day; and they that are found faithful, shall be called so. Perhaps they were censured by men, as <hi type="italic">righteous overmuch;</hi> but Christ will give them their just characters, of <hi type="italic">good and faithful.</hi> 2. Their performances will be accepted; <hi type="italic">Well done.</hi> Christ will call those, and those only, <hi type="italic">good servants,</hi> that have done well; for it is <hi type="italic">by patient continuance in well-doing</hi> that we seek for this glory and honour; and if we seek, we shall find; if we do that which is good, and do it well, we shall have <hi type="italic">praise of the same.</hi> Some masters are so morose, that they will not commend their servants, though they do their work ever so well; it is thought enough not to chide: but Christ will commend his servants that do well; whether their praise be of men or not, it is of him; and if we have the good word of our Master, the matter is not great what our fellow-servants say of us; if he saith, <hi type="italic">Well done,</hi> we are happy, and it should then be a small thing to us to be judged of men's judgment; as, on the contrary, not he who commendeth himself, or whom his neighbours commend, is approved, but whom the Lord commends. <div eID="gen23737" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23738" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> He rewards them. The faithful servants of Christ shall not be put off with bare commendation; no, all their work and labour of love shall be rewarded. <div eID="gen23738" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23739" type="x-p"/> Now this reward is here expressed two ways. <div eID="gen23739" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23740" type="x-p"/> 1. In one expression agreeable to the parable; <hi type="italic">Thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things.</hi> It is usual in the courts of princes, and families of great men, to advance those to higher offices, that have been faithful in lower. Note, Christ is a master that will prefer his servants who acquit themselves well. Christ has honour in store for those that honour him—<hi type="italic">a crown</hi> (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.8">2 Tim. iv. 8</reference>), <hi type="italic">a throne</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.21">Rev. iii. 21</reference>), <hi type="italic">a kingdom,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.25.34">ch. xxv. 34</reference>. Here they are beggars; in heaven they shall be rulers. The upright shall have dominion: Christ's servants are all princes. <div eID="gen23740" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23741" type="x-p"/> Observe the disproportion between the work and the reward; there are but few things in which the saints are serviceable to the glory of God, but there are many things wherein they shall be glorified with God. What charge we receive from God, what work we do for God in this world, is but little, very little, compared with <hi type="italic">the joy set before us.</hi> Put together all our service, all our sufferings, all our improvements, all the good we do to others, all we get to ourselves, and they are but a few things, next to nothing, not worthy to be compared, not fit to be named the same day with the glory to be revealed. <div eID="gen23741" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23742" type="x-p"/> 2. In another expression, which slips out of the parable into the thing signified by it; <hi type="italic">Enter thou into the joy of thy Lord.</hi> Note, (1.) The state of the blessed is a state of joy, not only because all tears shall then be wiped away, but all the springs of comfort shall be opened to them, and the fountains of joy broken up. Where there are the vision and fruition of God, a perfection of holiness, and the society of the blessed, there cannot but be a fulness of joy. (2.) This joy is the <hi type="italic">joy of their Lord;</hi> the joy which he himself has purchased and provided for them; the joy of the redeemed, bought with the sorrow of the Redeemer. It is the joy which he himself is in the possession of, and which he had his eye upon when he <hi type="italic">endured the cross, and despised the shame,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.12.2">Heb. xii. 2</reference>. It is the joy of which he himself is the fountain and centre. It is the joy of our Lord, for it is <hi type="italic">joy in the Lord,</hi> who is our exceeding joy. Abraham was not willing that the <hi type="italic">steward of his house,</hi> though <hi type="italic">faithful,</hi> should be <hi type="italic">his heir</hi> (<reference osisRef="Gen.15.3">Gen. xv. 3</reference>); but Christ admits his faithful stewards into his own joy, to be joint-heirs with him. (3.) Glorified saints shall enter into this joy, shall have a full and complete possession of it, as the heir when he comes of age enters upon his estate, or as they that were ready, <hi type="italic">went</hi> in to the marriage feast. Here the joy of our Lord enters into the saints, in the earnest of the Spirit; shortly they shall enter into it, shall be in it to eternity, as in their element. <div eID="gen23742" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23743" type="x-p"/> (2.) The bad account of the slothful servant. Observe, <div eID="gen23743" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23744" type="x-p"/> [1.] His apology for himself, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.24-Matt.25.25">v. 24, 25</reference>. Though he had received but <hi type="italic">one</hi> talent, for that one he is called to account. The smallness of our receiving will not excuse us from a reckoning. None shall be called to an account for more than they have received; but for what we have, we must all account. <div eID="gen23744" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23745" type="x-p"/> Observe, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> What he confides in. He comes to the account with a deal of assurance, relying on the plea he had to put in, that he was able to say, "<hi type="italic">Lo, there thou hast that is thine;</hi> if I have not made it more, as the others have done, yet this I can say, I have not made it less." This, he thinks, may serve to bring him off, if not with praise, yet with safety. <div eID="gen23745" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23746" type="x-p"/> Note, Many a one goes very securely to judgment, presuming upon the validity of a plea that will be overruled as vain and frivolous. Slothful professors, that are afraid of doing too much for God, yet hope to come off as well as those that take so much pains in religion. Thus <hi type="italic">the sluggard is wiser in his own conceit than seven men that can render a reason,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.26.16">Prov. xxvi. 16</reference>. This servant thought that his account would pass well enough, because he could say, <hi type="italic">There thou hast that is thine.</hi> "Lord, I was no spendthrift of my estate, no prodigal of my time, no profaner of my sabbaths, no opposer of good ministers and good preaching; Lord, I never ridiculed my bible, nor set my wits to work to banter religion, nor abused my power to persecute any good man; I never drowned my parts, nor wasted God's good creatures in drunkenness and gluttony, nor ever to my knowledge did I injury to any body." Many that are called Christians, build great hopes for heaven upon their being able to make such an account; yet all this amounts to no more than <hi type="italic">there thou hast that is thine;</hi> as if no more were required, or could be expected. <div eID="gen23746" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23747" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> What he confesses. He owns the burying of his talent; <hi type="italic">I hid thy talent in the earth.</hi> He speaks as if that were no great fault; nay, as if he deserved praise for his prudence in putting it in a safe place, and running no hazards with it. Note, It is common for people to make a very light matter of that which will be their condemnation in the great day. Or, if he was conscious to himself that it was his fault, it intimates how easily slothful servants will be convicted in the judgment; there will need no great search for proof, for <hi type="italic">their own tongues shall fall upon them.</hi> <div eID="gen23747" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23748" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> What he makes his excuse; <hi type="italic">I knew that thou were a hard man, and I was afraid.</hi> Good thought of God would beget love, and that love would make us diligent and faithful; but hard thoughts of God beget fear, and that fear makes us slothful and unfaithful. His excuse bespeaks, <div eID="gen23748" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23749" type="x-p"/> 1. The sentiments of an enemy; <hi type="italic">I knew thee, that thou art a hard man.</hi> This was like that wicked saying of the house of Israel, <hi type="italic">The way of the Lord is not equal,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ezek.18.25">Ezek. xviii. 25</reference>. Thus his <hi type="italic">de</hi>fence is his <hi type="italic">of</hi>fence. <hi type="italic">The foolishness of man perverteth his way,</hi> and then, as if that would mend the matter, <hi type="italic">his heart fretteth against the Lord.</hi> This is covering the transgression, as Adam, who implicitly laid the fault on God himself; <hi type="italic">The woman which thou gavest me.</hi> Note, Carnal hearts are apt to conceive false and wicked opinions concerning God, and with them to harden themselves in their evil ways. Observe how confidently he speaks; <hi type="italic">I knew thee to be so.</hi> How could he know him to be so? <hi type="italic">What iniquity have we or our fathers found in him?</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.2.5">Jer. ii. 5</reference>. Wherein has he wearied us with his work, or deceived us in his wages? <reference osisRef="Mic.6.3">Mic. vi. 3</reference>. Has he <hi type="italic">been a wilderness to us, or a land of darkness?</hi> Thus long God has governed the world, and may ask with more reason than Samuel himself could, <hi type="italic">Whom have I defrauded? or whom have I oppressed?</hi> Does not all the world know the contrary, that he is so far from being a hard master, that <hi type="italic">the earth is full of his goodness,</hi> so far from reaping where he sowed not, that he sows a great deal where he reaps nothing? For he <hi type="italic">causes the sun to shine, and his rain to fall, upon the evil and unthankful, and fills their hearts with food and gladness</hi> who say to the Almighty, <hi type="italic">Depart from us.</hi> This suggestion bespeaks the common reproach which wicked people cast upon God, as if all the blame of their sin and ruin lay at his door, for denying them his grace; whereas it is certain that never any who faithfully improved the common grace they had, perished for want of special grace; nor can any show what could in reason have been done more for an unfruitful vineyard than God has done in it. God does not demand brick, and deny straw; no, whatever is required in the covenant, is promised in the covenant; so that if we perish, it is owing to ourselves. <div eID="gen23749" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23750" type="x-p"/> 2. The spirit of a slave; <hi type="italic">I was afraid,</hi> This ill affection toward God arose from his false notions of him; and nothing is more unworthy of God, nor more hinders our duty to him, than slavish fear. This has bondage and torment, and is directly opposite to that entire love which the great commandment requires. Note, Hard thoughts of God drive us from, and cramp us in his service. Those who think it impossible to please him, and in vain to serve him, will do nothing to purpose in religion. <div eID="gen23750" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23751" type="x-p"/> [2.] His Lord's answer to this apology. His plea will stand him in no stead, it is overruled, nay, it is made to turn against him, and he is struck speechless with it; for here we have his conviction and his condemnation. <div eID="gen23751" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23752" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> His conviction, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.26-Matt.25.27">v. 26, 27</reference>. Two things he is convicted of. <div eID="gen23752" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23753" type="x-p"/> 1. Slothfulness; <hi type="italic">Thou wicked and slothful servant.</hi> Note, Slothful servants are wicked servants, and will be reckoned with as such by their master, for he that is <hi type="italic">slothful in his work,</hi> and neglects the good that God has commanded, <hi type="italic">is brother to him that is a great waster,</hi> by doing the evil that God has forbidden, <reference osisRef="Prov.18.9">Prov. xviii. 9</reference>. He that is careless in God's work, is near akin to him that is busy in the devil's work. <hi type="italic">Satis est mali nihil fecisse boni—To do no good is to incur very serious blame.</hi> Omissions are sins, and must come into judgment; slothfulness makes way for wickedness; all become <hi type="italic">filthy,</hi> for <hi type="italic">there is none that doeth good,</hi> <reference osisRef="Ps.14.3">Ps. xiv. 3</reference>. When the house is empty, the unclean spirit takes possession. Those that are idle in the affairs of their souls, are not only idle, but something worse, <reference osisRef="1Tim.5.13">1 Tim. v. 13</reference>. When men sleep, the enemy sows tares. <div eID="gen23753" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23754" type="x-p"/> 2. Self-contradiction (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.26-Matt.25.27">v. 26, 27</reference>); <hi type="italic">Thou knewest that I reap where I sowed not: thou oughtest therefore to have put my money to the exchangers.</hi> Note, The hard thoughts which sinners have of God, though false and unjust, will be so far from justifying their wickedness and slothfulness, that they will rather aggravate and add to their guilt. Three ways this may be taken; (1.) "Suppose I had been so hard a master, shouldest not thou therefore have been the more diligent and careful to please me, if not for <hi type="italic">love,</hi> yet for <hi type="italic">fear,</hi> and for that reason oughtest not thou to have minded thy work?" If our God is a consuming fire, in consideration of that let us study how to serve him. Or thus, (2.) "If thou didst think me to be a hard master, and therefore durst not trade with the money thyself, for fear of losing by it, and being made to stand to the loss, yet thou mightest have put it into the hands of the exchangers, or goldsmith, mightest have brought it into the bank, and then at my coming, if I could not have had the greater improvement, by trade and merchandize (as of the other talents), yet I might have had the less improvement, of bare interest, and should have received <hi type="italic">my own with usury;</hi>" which, it seems, was a common practice at that time, and not disallowed by our Saviour. Note, If we could not, or durst not, do what we would, yet that excuse will not serve, when it will be made to appear that we did not do what we could and durst. If we could not find in our hearts to venture upon more difficult and hazardous services, yet will that justify us in shrinking from those that were more safe and easy? Something is better than nothing; if we fail of showing our courage in bold enterprises, yet we must not fail to testify our good will in honest endeavours; and our Master <hi type="italic">will not despise the day of small things.</hi> Or thus, (3.) "Suppose I did reap <hi type="italic">where I sowed not,</hi> yet that is nothing to thee, for I had sowed upon thee, and the talent was my money which thou wast entrusted with, not only to keep, but to improve." Note, In the day of account, wicked and slothful servants will be left quite without excuse; frivolous pleas will be overruled, and every mouth will be stopped; and those who now stand so much upon their own justification will not have one word to say for themselves. <div eID="gen23754" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23755" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> His condemnation. The slothful servant is sentenced, <div eID="gen23755" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23756" type="x-p"/> 1. To be deprived of his talent (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.28-Matt.25.29">v. 28, 29</reference>); <hi type="italic">Take therefore the talent from him.</hi> The talents were first disposed of by the Master, as an absolute Owner, but this was now disposed of by him as a Judge; he takes it from the unfaithful servant, to punish him, and gives it to him that was eminently faithful, to reward him. And the meaning of this part of the parable we have in the reason of the sentence (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.29">v. 29</reference>), <hi type="italic">To every one that hath shall be given.</hi> This may be applied, (1.) To the blessings of this life—worldly wealth and possessions. These we are entrusted with, to be used for the glory of God, and the good of those about us. Now <hi type="italic">he that hath</hi> these things, and useth them for these ends, he <hi type="italic">shall have abundance;</hi> perhaps abundance of the things themselves, at least, abundance of comfort in them, and of better things; but <hi type="italic">from him that hath not,</hi> that is, that hath these things as if he had them not, had not power to eat of them, or to do good with (<hi type="italic">Avaro deest, tam quod habet, quam quod non habet—The miser may be considered as destitute of what he has, as well as of what he has not</hi>), they <hi type="italic">shall be taken away.</hi> Solomon explains this, <reference osisRef="Prov.11.24">Prov. xi. 24</reference>. <hi type="italic">There is that scattereth, and yet increaseth; and there is that withholdeth more than is meet, and it tendeth to poverty.</hi> Giving to the poor is trading with what we have, and the returns will be rich; it will multiply the meal in the barrel, and the oil in the cruse: but those that are sordid, and niggardly, and uncharitable, will find that those riches which are so got, <hi type="italic">perish by evil travail,</hi> <reference osisRef="Eccl.5.13-Eccl.5.14">Eccl. v. 13, 14</reference>. Sometimes Providence strangely transfers estates from those that do no good with them to those that do; they are <hi type="italic">gathered for him that will pity the poor,</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.28.8">Prov. xxviii. 8</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Prov.13.22">Prov. xiii. 22</reference>; <reference osisRef="Job.27.16-Job.27.17">Job xxvii. 16, 17</reference>; <reference osisRef="Eccl.2.26">Eccl. ii. 26</reference>. (2.) We may apply it to the means of grace. They who are diligent in improving the opportunities they have, God will enlarge them, will <hi type="italic">set before them an open door</hi> (<reference osisRef="Rev.3.8">Rev. iii. 8</reference>); but they who know not the day of their visitation, shall have the things that belong to their peace hid from their eyes. For proof of this, <hi type="italic">go see what God did to Shiloh,</hi> <reference osisRef="Jer.7.12">Jer. vii. 12</reference>. (3.) We may apply it to the common gifts of the Spirit. He that hath these, and doeth good with them, shall have abundance; these gifts improve by exercise, and brighten by being used; the more we do, the more we may do, in religion; but those who stir not up the gift that is in them, who do not exert themselves according to their capacity, their gifts rust, and decay, and go out like a neglected fire. From his that hath not a living principle of grace in his soul, shall be taken away the common gifts which he hath, as the lamps of the foolish virgins went out for want of oil, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.8">v. 8</reference>. Thus the arm of the <hi type="italic">idle shepherd,</hi> which he had sluggishly folded up in his bosom, comes to be dried up, and his right eye, which he had carelessly or wilfully shut, becomes utterly darkened, as it is threatened, <reference osisRef="Zech.11.17">Zech. xi. 17</reference>. <div eID="gen23756" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23757" type="x-p"/> 2. He is sentenced to be <hi type="italic">cast into outer darkness,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.25.30">v. 30</reference>. Here, <div eID="gen23757" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23758" type="x-p"/> (1.) His character is that of an <hi type="italic">unprofitable servant.</hi> Note, Slothful servants will be reckoned with as unprofitable servants, who do nothing to the purpose of their coming into the world, nothing to answer the end of their birth or baptism, who are no way serviceable to the glory of God, the good of others, or the salvation of their own souls. A slothful servant is a withered member in the body, a barren tree in the vineyard, an idle drone in the hive, he is good for nothing. In one sense, we are all <hi type="italic">unprofitable servants</hi> (<reference osisRef="Luke.17.10">Luke xvii. 10</reference>); we cannot <hi type="italic">profit God,</hi> <reference osisRef="Job.22.2">Job xxii. 2</reference>. But to others, and to ourselves, it is required that we be profitable; if we be not, Christ will not own us as his servants: it is not enough not to do hurt, but we must do good, must bring forth fruit, and though thereby God is not profited, yet he is glorified, <reference osisRef="John.15.8">John xv. 8</reference>. <div eID="gen23758" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23759" type="x-p"/> (2.) His doom is, to be <hi type="italic">cast into outer darkness.</hi> Here, as in what was said to the faithful servants, our Saviour slides insensibly out of the parable into the thing intended by it, and it serves as a key to the whole; for, <hi type="italic">outer darkness, where there is weeping and gnashing of teeth,</hi> is, in Christ's discourses, the common periphrasis of the miseries of the damned in hell. Their state is, [1.] Very dismal; it is outer darkness. Darkness is uncomfortable and frightful: it was one of the plagues of Egypt. In hell there are <hi type="italic">chains of darkness,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Pet.2.4">2 Pet. ii. 4</reference>. In the dark <hi type="italic">no man can work,</hi> a fit punishment for a slothful servant. It is <hi type="italic">outer</hi> darkness, <hi type="italic">out</hi> from the light of heaven, <hi type="italic">out</hi> from the joy of their Lord, into which the faithful servants were admitted; <hi type="italic">out</hi> from the feast. Compare <reference osisRef="Matt.8.12">ch. viii. 12</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.22.13">xxii. 13</reference>. [2.] Very doleful; there is weeping, which bespeaks great sorrow, and gnashing of teeth, which bespeaks great vexation and indignation. This will be the portion of the slothful servant.
