entries.61182eb4cd134b419be1a82d11f468ec6262d990: <div eID="gen23759" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3">The Process of the Last Judgment.</title> <div sID="gen23760" type="x-p"/> <hi type="super">31</hi> When the Son of man shall come in his glory, and all the holy angels with him, then shall he sit upon the throne of his glory: <hi type="super">32</hi> And before him shall be gathered all nations: and he shall separate them one from another, as a shepherd divideth <hi type="italic">his</hi> sheep from the goats: <hi type="super">33</hi> And he shall set the sheep on his right hand, but the goats on the left. <hi type="super">34</hi> Then shall the King say unto them on his right hand, Come, ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world: <hi type="super">35</hi> For I was an hungred, and ye gave me meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me drink: I was a stranger, and ye took me in: <hi type="super">36</hi> Naked, and ye clothed me: I was sick, and ye visited me: I was in prison, and ye came unto me. 37 Then shall the righteous answer him, saying, Lord, when saw we thee an hungred, and fed <hi type="italic">thee?</hi> or thirsty, and gave <hi type="italic">thee</hi> drink? <hi type="super">38</hi> When saw we thee a stranger, and took <hi type="italic">thee</hi> in? or naked, and clothed <hi type="italic">thee?</hi> <hi type="super">39</hi> Or when saw we thee sick, or in prison, and came unto thee? <hi type="super">40</hi> And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye have done <hi type="italic">it</hi> unto one of the least of these my brethren, ye have done <hi type="italic">it</hi> unto me. <hi type="super">41</hi> Then shall he say also unto them on the left hand, Depart from me, ye cursed, into everlasting fire, prepared for the devil and his angels: 42 For I was an hungred, and ye gave me no meat: I was thirsty, and ye gave me no drink: <hi type="super">43</hi> I was a stranger, and ye took me not in: naked, and ye clothed me not: sick, and in prison, and ye visited me not. <hi type="super">44</hi> Then shall they also answer him, saying, Lord, when saw we thee an hungred, or athirst, or a stranger, or naked, or sick, or in prison, and did not minister unto thee? <hi type="super">45</hi> Then shall he answer them, saying, Verily I say unto you, Inasmuch as ye did <hi type="italic">it</hi> not to one of the least of these, ye did <hi type="italic">it</hi> not to me. <hi type="super">46</hi> And these shall go away into everlasting punishment: but the righteous into life eternal. <div eID="gen23760" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23761" type="x-p"/> We have here a description of the process of the last judgment in the great day. There are some passages in it that are parabolical; as the separating between the sheep and the goats, and the dialogues between the judge and the persons judged: but there is no thread of similitude carried through the discourse, and therefore it is rather to be called a draught or delineation of the final judgment, than a parable; it is, as it were, the explanation of the former parables. And here we have, <div eID="gen23761" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23762" type="x-p"/> I. The placing of the judge upon the judgment-seat (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.31">v. 31</reference>); <hi type="italic">When the Son of man shall come.</hi> Observe here, <div eID="gen23762" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23763" type="x-p"/> 1. That there is a judgment to come, in which every man shall be sentenced to a state of everlasting happiness, or misery, in the world of recompence or retribution, according to what he did in this world of trial and probation, which is to be judged of by the rule of the everlasting gospel. <div eID="gen23763" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23764" type="x-p"/> 2. The administration of the judgment of the great day is committed to the Son of man; for by him God will judge the world (<reference osisRef="Acts.17.31">Acts xvii. 31</reference>), and to him all judgment is committed, and therefore the judgment of that day, which is the centre of all. Here, as elsewhere, when the last judgment is spoken of, Christ is called <hi type="italic">the son of man,</hi> because he is to judge the sons of men (and, being himself of the same nature, he is the more unexceptionable); and because his wonderful condescension to take upon him our nature, and to become the son of man, will be recompensed by this exaltation in that day, and an honour put upon the human nature. <div eID="gen23764" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23765" type="x-p"/> 3. Christ's appearing to judge the world will be splendid and glorious. Agrippa and Bernice came to the judgment-seat with <hi type="italic">great pomp</hi> (<reference osisRef="Acts.25.23">Acts xxv. 23</reference>); but that was (as the original word is) <hi type="italic">great fancy.</hi> Christ will come to the judgment-seat in real glory: the Sun of righteousness shall then shine in his meridian lustre, and the Prince of the kings of the earth shall show the riches of his glorious kingdom, and the honours of his excellent majesty; and all the world shall see what the saints only do now believe—that he is the brightness of his Father's glory. He shall come not only in the glory of his Father, but in his own glory, as mediator: his first coming was under a black cloud of obscurity; his second will be in a bright cloud of glory. The assurance Christ gave his disciples of his future glory, might help to take off the offence of the cross, and his approaching disgrace and suffering. <div eID="gen23765" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23766" type="x-p"/> 4. When Christ comes in his glory to judge the world, he will bring all his holy angels with him. This glorious person will have a glorious retinue, his holy myriads, who will be not only his attendants, but ministers of his justice; they shall come with him both for state and service. They must come to call the court (<reference osisRef="1Thess.4.16">1 Thess. iv. 16</reference>), to gather the elect (<reference osisRef="Matt.24.31">ch. xxiv. 31</reference>), to bundle the tares (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.40">ch. xiii. 40</reference>), to be witnesses of the saints' glory (<reference osisRef="Luke.12.8">Luke xii. 8</reference>), and of sinners' misery, <reference osisRef="Rev.14.10">Rev. xiv. 10</reference>. <div eID="gen23766" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23767" type="x-p"/> 5. He will then sit upon the throne of his glory. He is <hi type="italic">now</hi> set down with the Father upon his throne; and it is a throne of grace, to which we may come boldly; it is a throne of government, the throne of his father David; he is a priest upon that throne: but <hi type="italic">then</hi> he will sit upon the throne of glory, the throne of judgment. See <reference osisRef="Dan.7.9-Dan.7.10">Dan. vii. 9, 10</reference>. Solomon's throne, though there was not its like in any kingdom, was but a dunghill to it. Christ, in the days of his flesh, was arraigned as a prisoner at the bar; but at his second coming, he will sit as a judge upon the bench. <div eID="gen23767" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23768" type="x-p"/> II. The appearing of all the children of men before him (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.32">v. 32</reference>); <hi type="italic">Before him shall be gathered all nations.</hi> Note, The judgment of the great day will be a general judgment. All must be summoned before Christ's tribunal; all of every age of the world, from the beginning to the end of time; all of every place on earth, even from the remotest corners of the world, most obscure, and distant from each other; all nations, all those nations of men that are made of one blood, to dwell on all the face of the earth. <div eID="gen23768" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23769" type="x-p"/> III. The distinction that will then be made between the precious and the vile; <hi type="italic">He shall separate them one from another,</hi> as the tares and wheat are separated at the harvest, the good fish and the bad at the shore, the corn and chaff in the floor. Wicked and godly here dwell together in the same kingdoms, cities, churches, families, and are not certainly distinguishable one from another; such are the infirmities of saints, such the hypocrisies of sinners, and one event to both: but in that day they will be separated, and parted for ever; <hi type="italic">Then shall ye return, and discern between the righteous and the wicked,</hi> <reference osisRef="Mal.3.18">Mal. iii. 18</reference>. They cannot separate themselves one from another in this world (<reference osisRef="1Cor.5.10">1 Cor. v. 10</reference>), nor can any one else separate them (<reference osisRef="Matt.13.29">ch. xiii. 29</reference>); but the Lord knows them that are his, and he can separate them. This separation will be so exact, that the most inconsiderable saints shall not be lost in the crowd of sinners, nor the most plausible sinner hid in the crowd of saints (<reference osisRef="Ps.1.5">Ps. i. 5</reference>), but every one shall go to his own place. This is compared to a shepherd's dividing between the sheep and the goats; it is taken from <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.17">Ezek. xxxiv. 17</reference>, <hi type="italic">Behold, I judge between cattle and cattle.</hi> Note, 1. Jesus Christ is the great Shepherd; he now feeds his flock like a shepherd, and will shortly distinguish between those that are his, and those that are not, as Laban divided his sheep from Jacob's, and set three days' journey between them, <reference osisRef="Gen.30.35-Gen.30.36">Gen. xxx. 35, 36</reference>. 2. The godly are like sheep—innocent, mild, patient, useful: the wicked are like goats, a baser kind of animal, unsavoury and unruly. The sheep and goats are here feeding all day in the same pasture, but will be coted at night in different folds. Being thus divided, he will set the <hi type="italic">sheep on his right hand,</hi> and the <hi type="italic">goats on his left,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.25.33">v. 33</reference>. Christ puts honour upon the godly, as we show respect to those we set on our right hand; but the wicked shall rise to everlasting shame, <reference osisRef="Dan.12.2">Dan. xii. 2</reference>. It is not said that he shall put the rich on his right hand, and the poor on his left; the learned and noble on his right hand, and unlearned and despised on his left; but the godly on his right hand, and the wicked on his left. All other divisions and subdivisions will then be abolished; but the great distinction of men into saints and sinners, sanctified and unsanctified, will remain for ever, and men's eternal state will be determined by it. The wicked took up with left-handed blessings, riches and honour, and so shall their doom be. <div eID="gen23769" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23770" type="x-p"/> IV. The process of the judgement concerning each of these. <div eID="gen23770" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23771" type="x-p"/> 1. Concerning the godly, on the right hand. Their cause must be first despatched, that they may be assessors with Christ in the judgement of the wicked, whose misery will be aggravated by their seeing Abraham, and Isaac, and Jacob, admitted into the kingdom of heaven, <reference osisRef="Luke.13.28">Luke xiii. 28</reference>. Observe here, <div eID="gen23771" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23772" type="x-p"/> (1.) The <hi type="italic">glory</hi> conferred upon them; the sentence by which they shall be not only acquitted, but preferred and rewarded (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.34">v. 34</reference>); <hi type="italic">The king shall say unto them.</hi> He that was the Shepherd (which bespeaks the care and tenderness wherewith he will make this disquisition), is here the King, which bespeaks the authority wherewith he will then pronounce the sentence: where the word of this King is, there is power. Here are two things in this sentence: <div eID="gen23772" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23773" type="x-p"/> [1.] The acknowledging of the saints to be the blessed of the Lord; <hi type="italic">Come, ye blessed of my Father. First,</hi> He pronounces them <hi type="italic">blessed;</hi> and his saying they are blessed, makes them so. The law curses them for their many discontinuances; but Christ having redeemed them from the curse of the law, and purchased a blessing for them, commands a blessing on them. <hi type="italic">Secondly, Blessed of his Father;</hi> reproached and cursed by the world, but blessed of God. As the Spirit glorifies the Son (<reference osisRef="John.16.14">John xvi. 14</reference>), so the Son glorifies the Father by referring the salvation of the saints to him as the First Cause; all our blessings in heavenly things flow to us from God, as the Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.3">Eph. i. 3</reference>. <hi type="italic">Thirdly,</hi> He calls them <hi type="italic">to come:</hi> this <hi type="italic">come</hi> is, in effect, "<hi type="italic">Welcome,</hi> ten thousand welcomes, to the blessings of my father; come to me, come to be for ever with me; you that followed me bearing the cross, now come along with me wearing the crown. The blessed of my Father are the beloved of my soul, that have been too long at a distance from me; come, now, come into my bosom, come into my arms, come into my dearest embraces!" O with what joy will this fill the hearts of the saints in that day! We now come boldly to the throne of grace, but we shall then come boldly to the throne of glory; and this word holds out the golden sceptre, with an assurance that our requests shall be granted to more than the half of the kingdom. Now the Spirit saith, <hi type="italic">Come,</hi> in the word; and the bride saith, <hi type="italic">Come,</hi> in prayer; and the result hereof is a sweet communion: but the perfection of bliss will be, when <hi type="italic">the King shall say, Come.</hi> <div eID="gen23773" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23774" type="x-p"/> [2.] The admission of the saints into the blessedness and kingdom of the Father; <hi type="italic">Inherit the kingdom prepared for you.</hi> <div eID="gen23774" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23775" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> the happiness they shall be possessed of is very rich; we are told what it is by him who had reason to know it, having purchased it for them, and possessed it himself. <div eID="gen23775" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23776" type="x-p"/> 1. It is a <hi type="italic">kingdom;</hi> which is reckoned the most valuable possession on earth, and includes the greatest wealth and honour. Those that inherit kingdoms, wear all the glories of the crown, enjoy all the pleasures of the court, and command the peculiar treasures of the provinces; yet this is but a faint resemblance of the felicities of the saints in heaven. They that here are beggars, prisoners, accounted as the off-scouring of all things, shall then inherit a kingdom, <reference osisRef="Ps.113.7">Ps. cxiii. 7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.2.26-Rev.2.27">Rev. ii. 26, 27</reference>. <div eID="gen23776" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23777" type="x-p"/> 2. It is a kingdom <hi type="italic">prepared:</hi> the happiness must needs be great, for it is the product of the divine counsels. Note, There is great preparation made for the entertainment of the saints in the kingdom of glory. The Father designed it for them in his thoughts of love, and provided it for them in the greatness of his wisdom and power. The Son purchased it for them, and is entered as the fore-runner to prepare a place, <reference osisRef="John.14.2">John xiv. 2</reference>. And the blessed Spirit, in preparing them for the kingdom, in effect, is preparing it for them. <div eID="gen23777" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23778" type="x-p"/> 3. It is prepared <hi type="italic">for them.</hi> This bespeaks, (1.) The suitableness of this happiness; it is in all points adapted to the nature of a soul, and to the new nature of a sanctified soul. (2.) Their property and interest in it. It is prepared on purpose for them; not only for such as you, but for you, you by name, you personally and particularly, who were chosen to salvation through sanctification. <div eID="gen23778" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23779" type="x-p"/> 4. It is prepared <hi type="italic">from the foundation of the world.</hi> This happiness was designed for the saints, and they for it, before time began, from all eternity, <reference osisRef="Eph.1.4">Eph. i. 4</reference>. The end, which is last in execution, is first in intention. Infinite Wisdom had an eye to the eternal glorification of the saints, from the first founding of the creation: <hi type="italic">All things are for your sakes,</hi> <reference osisRef="2Cor.4.15">2 Cor. iv. 15</reference>. Or, it denotes the preparation of the place of this happiness, which is to be the seat and habitation of the blessed, in the very beginning of the work of creation, <reference osisRef="Gen.1.1">Gen. i. 1</reference>. There in the heaven of heavens the morning stars were singing together, when the foundations of the earth were fastened, <reference osisRef="Job.38.4-Job.38.7">Job xxxviii. 4-7</reference>. <div eID="gen23779" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23780" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The tenure by which they shall hold and possess it is very good, they shall come and <hi type="italic">inherit it.</hi> What we come to by inheritance, is not got by any procurement of our own, but purely, as the lawyers express it, <hi type="italic">by the act of God.</hi> It is God that makes heirs, heirs of heaven. We come to an inheritance by virtue of our sonship, our adoption; <hi type="italic">if children, then heirs.</hi> A title by inheritance is the sweetest and surest title; it alludes to possessions in the land of Canaan, which passed by inheritance, and would not be alienated longer than to the year of Jubilee. Thus is the heavenly inheritance indefeasible, and unalienable. Saints, in this world, are as heirs under age, tutored and governed till the time appointed of the Father (<reference osisRef="Gal.4.1-Gal.4.2">Gal. iv. 1, 2</reference>); and then they shall be put in full possession of that which now through grace they have a title to; <hi type="italic">Come,</hi> and inherit it. <div eID="gen23780" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23781" type="x-p"/> (2.) The ground of this (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.35-Matt.25.36">v. 35, 36</reference>), <hi type="italic">For I was an hungered, and ye gave me meat.</hi> We cannot hence infer that any good words of ours merit the happiness of heaven, by any intrinsic worth or excellency in them: our goodness extends not unto God; but it is plain that Jesus Christ will judge the world by the same rule by which he governs it, and therefore will reward those that have been obedient to that law; and mention will be made of their obedience, not as their title, but as their evidence of an interest in Christ, and his purchase. This happiness will be adjudged to obedient believers, not upon a <hi type="italic">quantum meruit—an estimate of merit,</hi> which supposes a proportion between the work and the reward, but upon the promise of God purchased by Jesus Christ, and the benefit of it secured under certain provisos and limitations; and it is the purchase and promise that give the title, the obedience is only the qualification of the person designed. An estate made by deed or will upon condition, when the condition is performed according to the true intent of the donor or testator, becomes absolute; and then, though the title be built purely upon the deed or will, yet the performing of the condition must be given in evidence: and so it comes in here; for Christ is the Author of eternal salvation to those only that obey him, and who patiently continue in well doing. <div eID="gen23781" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23782" type="x-p"/> Now the good works here mentioned are such as we commonly call works of charity to the poor: not but that many will be found on the right hand who never were in a capacity to feed the hungry, or clothe the naked, but were themselves fed and clothed by the charity of others; but one instance of sincere obedience is put for all the rest, and it teaches us this in general, that faith working by love is all in all in Christianity; <hi type="italic">Show me thy faith by thy works;</hi> and nothing will abound to a good account hereafter, but the fruits of righteousness in a good conversation now. The good works here described imply three things, which must be found in all that are saved. <div eID="gen23782" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23783" type="x-p"/> [1.] Self-denial, and contempt of the world; reckoning the things of the world no further good things, than as we are enabled to do good with them: and those who have not wherewithal to do good, must show the same disposition, by being contentedly and cheerfully poor. Those are fit for heaven that are mortified to the earth. <div eID="gen23783" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23784" type="x-p"/> [2.] Love to our brethren; which is the second great commandment, the fulfilling of the law, and an excellent preparative for the world of everlasting love. We must give proof of this love by our readiness to do good, and to communicate; good wishes are but mockeries without good works, <reference osisRef="Jas.2.15-Jas.2.16">Jam. ii. 15, 16</reference>; <reference osisRef="1John.3.17">1 John iii. 17</reference>. Those that have not to give, must show the same disposition some other way. <div eID="gen23784" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23785" type="x-p"/> [3.] A believing regard to Jesus Christ. That which is here rewarded is the relieving of the poor for Christ's sake, out of love to him, and with an eye to him. <hi type="italic">This</hi> puts an excellency upon the good work, when in it we serve the Lord Christ, which those may do that work for their own living, as well as those that help to keep others alive. See <reference osisRef="Eph.6.5-Eph.6.7">Eph. vi. 5-7</reference>. Those good works shall then be accepted which are done in the name of the Lord Jesus, <reference osisRef="Col.3.17">Col. iii. 17</reference>. <div eID="gen23785" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23786" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">I was hungry,</hi> that is, my disciples and followers were so, either by the persecutions of enemies for well-doing, or by the common dispensations of Providence; for in these things there is one event to the righteous and wicked: and <hi type="italic">you gave them meat.</hi> Note, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Providence so variously orders and disposes of the circumstances of his people in this world, as that while some are in a condition to give relief, others need it. It is no new thing for those that are feasted with the dainties of heaven to be hungry and thirsty, and to want daily food; for those that are at home in God, to be strangers in a strange land; for those that have put on Christ, to want clothes to keep them warm; for those that have healthful souls, to have sickly bodies; and for those to be in prison, that Christ has made free. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Works of charity and beneficence, according as our ability is, are necessary to salvation; and there will be more stress laid upon them in the judgment of the great day, than is commonly imagined; these must be the proofs of our love, and of our professed subjection to the gospel of Christ, <reference osisRef="2Cor.9.13">2 Cor. ix. 13</reference>. But they that show no mercy, shall have judgment without mercy. <div eID="gen23786" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23787" type="x-p"/> Now this reason is modestly excepted against by the righteous, but is explained by the Judge himself. <div eID="gen23787" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23788" type="x-p"/> 1. It is questioned by the righteous, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.37-Matt.25.39">v. 37-39</reference>. Not as if they were loth to inherit the kingdom, or were ashamed of their good deeds, or had not the testimony of their own consciences concerning them: but, (1.) The expressions are parabolical, designed to introduce and impress these great truths, that Christ has a mighty regard to works of charity, and is especially pleased with kindnesses done to his people for his sake. Or, (2.) They bespeak the humble admiration which glorified saints will be filled with, to find such poor and worthless services, as theirs are, so highly celebrated, and richly rewarded: <hi type="italic">Lord, when saw we thee an hungered, and fed thee?</hi> Note, Gracious souls are apt to think meanly of their own good deeds; especially as unworthy to be compared with the glory that shall be revealed. Far from this is the temper of those who said, <hi type="italic">Wherefore have we fasted, and thou seest not?</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.58.3">Isa. lviii. 3</reference>. Saints in heaven will wonder what brought them thither, and that God should so regard them and their services. It even put Nathanael to the blush, to hear Christ's encomium of him: <hi type="italic">Whence knowest thou me?</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.47-John.1.48">John i. 47, 48</reference>. See <reference osisRef="Eph.3.20">Eph. iii. 20</reference>. "<hi type="italic">When saw we thee an hungered?</hi> We have seen the poor in distress many a time; but when saw we thee?" Note, Christ is more among us than we think he is; surely the Lord is in this place, by his word, his ordinances, his ministers, his Spirit, yea, and his poor, and we know it not: <hi type="italic">When thou wert under the fig-tree, I saw thee,</hi> <reference osisRef="John.1.48">John i. 48</reference>. <div eID="gen23788" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23789" type="x-p"/> 2. It is explained by the Judge himself (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.40">v. 40</reference>); <hi type="italic">Inasmuch as ye have done it to these my brethren,</hi> to the least, to one of the least of them, <hi type="italic">ye have done it unto me.</hi> The good works of the saints, when they are produced in the great day, (1.) Shall all be remembered; and not the least, not one of the least, overlooked, no not a cup of cold water. (2.) They shall be interpreted most to their advantage, and the best construction that can be put upon them. As Christ makes the best of their infirmities, so he makes the most of their services. <div eID="gen23789" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23790" type="x-p"/> We see what recompences Christ has for those that feed the hungry, and clothe the naked; but what will become of the godly poor, that had not wherewithal to do so? Must they be shut out? No, [1.] Christ will own them, even the least of them, as his brethren; he will not be ashamed, nor think it any disparagement to him, <hi type="italic">to call them brethren,</hi> <reference osisRef="Heb.2.11">Heb. ii. 11</reference>. In the height of his glory, he will not disown his poor relations; Lazarus is there laid in his bosom, as a friend, as a brother. Thus he will confess them, <reference osisRef="Matt.10.32">ch. x. 32</reference>. [2.] He will take the kindness done to them, as done to himself; <hi type="italic">Ye have done it unto me;</hi> which shows a respect to the poor that were relieved, as well as to the rich that did relieve them. Note, Christ espouses his people's cause, and interests himself in their interests, and reckons himself received, and loved, and owned in them. If Christ himself were among us in poverty, how readily would we relieve him? In prison, how frequently would we visit him? We are ready to envy the honour they had, who ministered to him of their substance, <reference osisRef="Luke.8.3">Luke viii. 3</reference>. Wherever poor saints and poor ministers are, there Christ is ready to receive our kindnesses in them, and they shall be put to his account. <div eID="gen23790" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23791" type="x-p"/> 2. Here is the process concerning the wicked, those on the left hand. And in that we have, <div eID="gen23791" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23792" type="x-p"/> (1.) The sentence passed upon them, <reference osisRef="Matt.5.41">v. 41</reference>. It was a disgrace to be set on the left hand; but that is not the worst of it, he shall say to them, <hi type="italic">Depart from me, ye cursed.</hi> Every word has terror in it, like that of the trumpet at mount Sinai, waxing louder and louder, every accent more and more doleful, and exclusive of comfort. <div eID="gen23792" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23793" type="x-p"/> [1.] To be so near to Christ was some satisfaction, though under his frowns; but that will not be allowed, <hi type="italic">Depart from me.</hi> In this world they were often called to come to Christ, to come for life and rest, but they turned a deaf ear to his calls; justly therefore are they bid to depart from Christ, that would not come to him. "Depart from me the Fountain of all good, from me the Saviour, and therefore from all hope of salvation; I will never have any thing more to say to you, or do with you." Here they said to the Almighty, <hi type="italic">Depart from us;</hi> then he will <hi type="italic">choose their delusions,</hi> and say to them, <hi type="italic">Depart from me.</hi> Note, It is the hell of hell to depart from Christ. <div eID="gen23793" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23794" type="x-p"/> [2.] If they must depart, and depart from Christ, might they not be dismissed with a blessing, with one kind and compassionate word at least? No, <hi type="italic">Depart, ye cursed,</hi> They that would not come to Christ, to inherit a blessing, must depart from him under the burthen of a curse, that curse of the law on every one that breaks it, <reference osisRef="Gal.3.10">Gal. iii. 10</reference>. <hi type="italic">As they loved cursing, so it shall come unto them.</hi> But observe, The righteous are called <hi type="italic">the blessed of my Father;</hi> for their blessedness is owing purely to the grace of God and his blessing, but the wicked are called only <hi type="italic">ye cursed,</hi> for their damnation is of themselves. Hath God sold them? No, they have sold themselves, have laid themselves under the curse, <reference osisRef="Isa.50.1">Isa. l. 1</reference>. <div eID="gen23794" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23795" type="x-p"/> [3.] If they must depart, and depart with a curse, may they not go into some place of ease and rest? Will it not be misery enough for them to bewail their loss? No, there is a punishment of sense as well as loss; they must depart into <hi type="italic">fire,</hi> into torment as grievous as that of fire is to the body, and much more. This fire is the wrath of the eternal God fastening upon the guilty souls and consciences of sinners that have made themselves fuel for it. Our God is a consuming fire, and sinners fall immediately into his hands, <reference osisRef="Heb.10.31">Heb. x. 31</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rom.2.8-Rom.2.9">Rom. ii. 8, 9</reference>. <div eID="gen23795" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23796" type="x-p"/> [4.] If into fire, may it not be some light or gentle fire? No, it is <hi type="italic">prepared</hi> fire; it is a torment <hi type="italic">ordained of old,</hi> <reference osisRef="Isa.30.33">Isa. xxx. 33</reference>. The damnation of sinners is often spoken of as an act of the divine power; <hi type="italic">he is able to cast into hell.</hi> In the vessels of wrath he makes his power known; it is a <hi type="italic">destruction from the presence of the Lord, and from the glory of his power.</hi> In it shall be seen what a provoked God can do to make a provoking creature miserable. <div eID="gen23796" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23797" type="x-p"/> [5.] If into fire, prepared fire, O let it be but of short continuance, let them but pass <hi type="italic">through</hi> fire; no, the fire of God's wrath will be an <hi type="italic">everlasting</hi> fire; a fire, that, fastening and preying upon immortal souls, can never go out for want of fuel; and, being kindled and kept burning by the wrath of an immortal God, can never go out for want of being blown and stirred up; and, the streams of mercy and grace being for ever excluded, there is nothing to extinguish it. If a drop of water be denied to cool the tongue, buckets of water will never be granted to quench this flame. <div eID="gen23797" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23798" type="x-p"/> [6.] If they must be doomed to such a state of endless misery, yet may they not have some good company there? No, none but <hi type="italic">the devil and his angels,</hi> their sworn enemies, that helped to bring them to this misery, and will triumph over them in it. They served the devil while they lived, and therefore are justly sentenced to be where he is, as those that served Christ, are taken to be with him where he is. It is terrible to lie in a house haunted with devils; what will it be then to be companions with them for ever? Observe here, <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Christ intimates that there is one that is the prince of the devils, the ring-leader of the rebellion, and that the rest are his angels, his messengers, by whose agency he supports his kingdom. Christ and his angels will in that day triumph over the dragon and his, <reference osisRef="Rev.12.7-Rev.12.8">Rev. xii. 7, 8</reference>. <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> The fire is said to be prepared, not primarily for the wicked, as the kingdom is prepared for the righteous; but it was originally intended for <hi type="italic">the devil and his angels.</hi> If sinners make themselves associates with Satan by indulging their lusts, they may thank themselves if they become sharers in that misery which was prepared for him and his associates. Calvin notes upon this, that <hi type="italic">therefore</hi> the torment of the damned is said to be <hi type="italic">prepared for the devil and his angels,</hi> to cut off all hope of escaping it; the devil and his angels are already made prisoners in the pit, and can worms of the earth think to escape? <div eID="gen23798" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23799" type="x-p"/> (2.) The reason of this sentence assigned. God's judgments are all just, and he will be justified in them. He is Judge himself, and therefore <hi type="italic">the heavens shall declare his righteousness.</hi> <div eID="gen23799" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23800" type="x-p"/> Now, [1.] All that is charged upon them, on which the sentence is grounded, is, omission; as, before, the servant was condemned, not for wasting his talent, but for burying it; so here, he doth not say, "I was hungry and thirsty, for you took my meat and drink from me; I was a stranger, for you banished me; naked, for you stripped me; in prison, for you laid me there:" but, "When I was in these distresses, you were so selfish, so taken up with your own ease and pleasure, made so much of your labour, and were so loth to part with your money, that you did not <hi type="italic">minister</hi> as you might have done to my relief and succour. You were like those epicures that were at ease in Zion, and were not <hi type="italic">grieved for the affliction of Joseph,</hi>" <reference osisRef="Amos.6.4-Amos.6.6">Amos vi. 4-6</reference>. Note, Omissions are the ruin of thousands. <div eID="gen23800" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23801" type="x-p"/> [2.] It is the omission of works of charity to the poor. They are not sentenced for omitting their sacrifices and burnt-offerings (they abounded in these, <reference osisRef="Ps.50.8">Ps. l. 8</reference>), but for omitting the weightier matter of the law, <hi type="italic">judgment, mercy, and faith.</hi> The Ammonites and Moabites were excluded the sanctuary, because they <hi type="italic">met not Israel with bread and water,</hi> <reference osisRef="Deut.23.3-Deut.23.4">Deut. xxiii. 3, 4</reference>. Note, Uncharitableness to the poor is a damning sin. If we will not be brought to works of charity by the hope of reward, let us be influenced by fear of punishment; for <hi type="italic">they shall have judgment without mercy, that have showed no mercy.</hi> Observe, He doth not say, "I was sick, and you did not cure me; in prison, and you did not release me" (perhaps that was more than they could do); but, "You <hi type="italic">visited me not,</hi> which you might have done." Note, Sinners will be condemned, at the great day, for the omission of that good which it was in the power of their hand to do. But if the doom of the uncharitable be so dreadful, how much more intolerable will the doom of the cruel be, the doom of persecutors! Now this reason of the sentence is. <div eID="gen23801" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23802" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">First,</hi> Objected against by the prisoners (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.44">v. 44</reference>); <hi type="italic">Lord, when saw we thee an hungered, or athirst?</hi> Condemned sinners, though they have no plea that will bear them out, will yet in vain offer at excuses. Now. 1. The manner of their pleading bespeaks their present precipitation. They cut it short, as men in haste; <hi type="italic">when saw we thee hungry, or thirsty, or naked?</hi> They care not to repeat the charge, as conscious to themselves of their own guilt, and unable to bear the terrors of the judgment. Nor will they have time allowed them to insist upon such frivolous pleas; for it is all (as we say) but "trifling with the court." 2. The matter of their plea bespeaks their former inconsideration of that which they might have known, but would not till now that it was too late. They that had slighted and persecuted poor Christians, would not own that they had slighted and persecuted Christ: no, they never intended any affront to him, nor expected that so great a matter would have been made of it. They imagined it was only a company of poor, weak, silly, and contemptible people, who made more ado than needed about religion, that they put those slights upon; but they who do so, will be made to know, either in the day of their conversion, as Paul, or of their condemnation, as these here, that it was <hi type="italic">Jesus whom they persecuted.</hi> And, if they say, <hi type="italic">Behold, we knew it not: doth not he that pondereth the heart consider it?</hi> <reference osisRef="Prov.24.11-Prov.24.12">Prov. xxiv. 11, 12</reference>. <div eID="gen23802" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23803" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Secondly,</hi> Justified by the Judge, who will convince all the ungodly of the hard speeches spoken against him in those that are his, <reference osisRef="Jude.1.15">Jude 15</reference>. He goes by this rule (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.45">v. 45</reference>); <hi type="italic">Inasmuch as ye did it not to one of the least of these, ye did it not to me.</hi> Note, What is done against the faithful disciples and followers of Christ, even the least of them, he takes as done against himself. He is reproached and persecuted in them, for they are reproached and persecuted for his sake, and <hi type="italic">in all their afflictions he is afflicted.</hi> He that touches them, touches him in a part no less tender than the apple of his eye. <div eID="gen23803" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23804" type="x-p"/> <hi type="italic">Lastly,</hi> Here is the execution of both these sentences, <reference osisRef="Matt.25.46">v. 46</reference>. Execution is the life of the law, and Christ will take care that that be done according to the sentence. <div eID="gen23804" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23805" type="x-p"/> 1. <hi type="italic">The wicked shall go away into everlasting punishment.</hi> Sentence will then be executed speedily, and no reprieve granted, nor any time allowed to move in arrest of judgment. The execution of the wicked is first mentioned; for first the tares are gathered and burned. Note, (1.) The punishment of the wicked in the future state will be an everlasting punishment, for that state is an unalterable state. It can neither be thought that sinners should change their own natures, nor that God should give his grace to change them, when in this world the day of grace was misspent, the Spirit of grace resisted, and the means of grace abused and baffled. (2.) The wicked shall be made to <hi type="italic">go</hi> away into that punishment; not that they will go voluntarily, no, they are <hi type="italic">driven</hi> from light into darkness; but it bespeaks an irresistible conviction of guilt, and a final despair of mercy. <div eID="gen23805" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen23806" type="x-p"/> 2. <hi type="italic">The righteous shall go away into life eternal;</hi> that is, they shall <hi type="italic">inherit the kingdom,</hi> <reference osisRef="Matt.25.34">v. 34</reference>. Note, (1.) Heaven is life, it is all happiness. The life of the soul results from its union with God by the mediation of Jesus Christ, as that of the body from its union with the soul by the animal spirits. The heavenly life consists in the vision and fruition of God, in a perfect conformity to him, and an immediate uninterrupted communion with him. (2.) It is <hi type="italic">eternal</hi> life. There is no death to put a period to the life itself, nor old age to put a period to the comfort of it, or any sorrow to embitter it. Thus life and death, good and evil, the blessing and the curse, are set before us, that we may choose our way; and so shall our end be. Even the heathen had some notion of these different states of good and bad in the other world. Cicero in his <hi type="italic">Tusculan Questions,</hi> lib. 1, brings in Socrates thus speaking, <hi type="italic">Duæ sunt viæ, duplicesque cursus &#232; corpore exeuntium: nam qui se vitiis humanis contaminarunt, et libidinibus se tradiderunt, iis devium quoddam iter est, seclusum &#224; consilio deorum; qui autem se integros castosque servarunt, quibusque fuerit minima cum corporibus contagio, suntque in corporibus humanis vitam imitati deorum, iis ad illos a quibus sunt profecti facile patet reditus—Two paths open before those who depart out of the body. Such as have contaminated themselves with human vices, and yielded to their lusts, occupy a path that conducts them far from the assembly and council of the gods; but the upright and chaste, such as have been least defiled by the flesh, and have imitated, while in the body, the gods, these find it easy to return to the sublime beings from whom they came.</hi>  <chapter eID="Matt.25"/> <div eID="gen23806" type="x-p"/>

entries.5556ce281ad37fecf85295e106149fe151ee2cc8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13784"/><title type="x-s2">CHAPTER 25</title> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.25.1-Matt.25.13">Mt 25:1-13</reference>. Parable of the Ten Virgins.</title> <div sID="gen26449" type="x-p"/> This and the following parable are in Matthew alone.<div eID="gen26449" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26450" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13784"/><hi type="bold">1. Then--</hi>at the time referred to at the close of the preceding chapter, the time of the Lord's Second Coming to reward His faithful servants and take vengeance on the faithless. Then<div eID="gen26450" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26451" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">shall the kingdom of heaven be likened unto ten virgins, which took their lamps, and went forth to meet the bridegroom--</hi>This supplies a key to the parable, whose object is, in the main, the same as that of the last parable--to illustrate the vigilant and expectant attitude of faith, in respect of which believers are described as "they that look for Him" (<reference osisRef="Heb.9.28">He 9:28</reference>), and "love His appearing" (<reference osisRef="2Tim.4.8">2Ti 4:8</reference>). In the last parable it was that of servants waiting for their absent Lord; in this it is that of virgin attendants on a Bride, whose duty it was to go forth at night with lamps, and be ready on the appearance of the Bridegroom to conduct the Bride to his house, and go in with him to the marriage. This entire and beautiful change of figure brings out the lesson of the former parable in quite a new light. But let it be observed that, just as in the parable of the Marriage Supper (<reference osisRef="Luke.14.15-Luke.14.24">Lu 14:15-24</reference>), so in this--the Bride does not come into view at all in this parable; the Virgins and the Bridegroom holding forth all the intended instruction: nor could believers be represented both as Bride and Bridal Attendants without incongruity. <div eID="gen26451" type="x-p"/>
entries.90aa21c6a7c6cedf0677d4645b8e6daba8e23a74: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13785"/><div sID="gen26452" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13785"/><hi type="bold">2. And five of them were wise, and five were foolish--</hi>They are not distinguished into good and bad, as Trench observes, but into "wise" and "foolish"--just as in <reference osisRef="Matt.7.25-Matt.7.27">Mt 7:25-27</reference> those who reared their house for eternity are distinguished into "wise" and "foolish builders"; because in both cases a certain degree of goodwill towards the truth is assumed. To make anything of the equal number of both classes would, we think, be precarious, save to warn us how large a portion of those who, up to the last, so nearly resemble those that love Christ's appearing will be disowned by Him when He comes. <div eID="gen26452" type="x-p"/>
entries.3582c5b176168050bd17c7643e529873636c93ec: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13786"/><div sID="gen26453" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13786"/>3. They that were foolish took their lamps, and took no oil with them: <div eID="gen26453" type="x-p"/>
entries.e083a6812a2fe9bfee61c33223d97b69fcd74c86: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13787"/><div sID="gen26454" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13787"/><hi type="bold">4. But the wise took oil in their vessels with their lamps--</hi>What are these "lamps" and this "oil"? Many answers have been given. But since the foolish as well as the wise took their lamps and went forth with them to meet the Bridegroom, these lighted lamps and this advance a certain way in company with the wise, must denote that Christian profession which is common to all who bear the Christian name; while the insufficiency of this without something else, of which they never possessed themselves, shows that "the foolish" mean those who, with all that is common to them with real Christians, lack the essential preparation for meeting Christ. Then, since the wisdom of "the wise" consisted in their taking with their lamps a supply of oil in their vessels, keeping their lamps burning till the Bridegroom came, and so fitting them to go in with Him to the marriage, this supply of oil must mean that inward reality of grace which alone will stand when He appears whose eyes are as a flame of fire. But this is too general; for it cannot be for nothing that this inward grace is here set forth by the familiar symbol of oil, by which the Spirit of all grace is so constantly represented in Scripture. Beyond all doubt, this was what was symbolized by that precious anointing oil with which Aaron and his sons were consecrated to the priestly office (<reference osisRef="Exod.30.23-Exod.25.30">Ex 30:23-25, 30</reference>); by "the oil of gladness above His fellows" with which Messiah was to be anointed (<reference osisRef="Ps.45.7">Psa 45:7</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.1.9">He 1:9</reference>), even as it is expressly said, that "God giveth not the Spirit by measure unto Him" (<reference osisRef="John.3.34">Joh 3:34</reference>); and by the bowl full of golden oil, in Zechariah's vision, which, receiving its supplies from the two olive trees on either side of it, poured it through seven golden pipes into the golden lamp-stand to keep it continually burning bright (<reference osisRef="Zech.4.1-Zech.4.14">Zec 4:1-14</reference>)--for the prophet is expressly told that it was to proclaim the great truth, "Not by might, nor by power, but by My Spirit, saith the Lord of hosts [shall this temple be built]. Who art thou, O great mountain [of opposition to this issue]? Before Zerubbabel thou shalt become a plain [or, be swept out of the way], and he shall bring forth the head stone [of the temple], with shoutings [crying], Grace, Grace unto it." This supply of oil, then, representing that inward grace which distinguishes the wise, must denote, more particularly, that "supply of the Spirit of Jesus Christ," which, as it is the source of the new spiritual life at the first, is the secret of its enduring character. Everything short of this may be possessed by "the foolish"; while it is the possession of this that makes "the wise" to be "ready" when the Bridegroom appears, and fit to "go in with Him to the marriage." Just so in the parable of the Sower, the stony-ground hearers, "having no deepness of earth" and "no root in themselves" <reference osisRef="Matt.13.5">Mt 13:5</reference>; <reference osisRef="Mark.4.17">Mr 4:17</reference>), though they spring up and get even into ear, never ripen, while they in the good ground bear the precious grain. <div eID="gen26454" type="x-p"/>
entries.50a905cfb306c2939a07880088764a09b516f837: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13788"/><div sID="gen26455" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13788"/><hi type="bold">5. While the bridegroom tarried--</hi>So in <reference osisRef="Matt.24.48">Mt 24:48</reference>, "My Lord delayeth His coming"; and so Peter says sublimely of the ascended Saviour, "Whom the heaven must receive until the times of restitution of all things" (<reference osisRef="Acts.3.21">Ac 3:21</reference>, and compare <reference osisRef="Luke.19.11">Lu 19:11</reference>, <reference osisRef="Luke.19.12">12</reference>). Christ "tarries," among other reasons, to try the faith and patience of His people.<div eID="gen26455" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26456" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">they all slumbered and slept--</hi>the wise as well as the foolish. The world "slumbered" signifies, simply, "nodded," or, "became drowsy"; while the world "slept" is the usual word for lying down to sleep, denoting two stages of spiritual declension--first, that half-involuntary lethargy or drowsiness which is apt to steal over one who falls into inactivity; and then a conscious, deliberate yielding to it, after a little vain resistance. Such was the state alike of the wise and the foolish virgins, even till the cry of the Bridegroom's approach awoke them. So likewise in the parable of the Importunate Widow: "When the Son of man cometh, shall He find faith on the earth?" (<reference osisRef="Luke.18.8">Lu 18:8</reference>). <div eID="gen26456" type="x-p"/>
entries.d53d483627a7423db9e3362fa31ab164e4866a1a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13789"/><div sID="gen26457" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13789"/><hi type="bold">6. And at midnight--</hi>that is, the time when the Bridegroom will be least expected; for "the day of the Lord so cometh as a thief in the night" (<reference osisRef="1Thess.5.2">1Th 5:2</reference>).<div eID="gen26457" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26458" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there was a cry made, Behold, the Bridegroom cometh; go ye out to meet him--</hi>that is, Be ready to welcome Him. <div eID="gen26458" type="x-p"/>
entries.aee45ae02f6c40c0a2a25f048268b6fa23e0b28c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13790"/><div sID="gen26459" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13790"/><hi type="bold">7. Then all those virgins arose, and trimmed their lamps--</hi>the foolish virgins as well as the wise. How very long do both parties seem the same--almost to the moment of decision! Looking at the mere form of the parable, it is evident that the folly of "the foolish" consisted not in having no oil at all; for they must have had oil enough in their lamps to keep them burning up to this moment: their folly consisted in not making provision against its exhaustion, by taking with their lamp an oil-vessel wherewith to replenish their lamp from time to time, and so have it burning until the Bridegroom should come. Are we, then--with some even superior expositors--to conclude that the foolish virgins must represent true Christians as well as do the wise, since only true Christians have the Spirit, and that the difference between the two classes consists only in the one having the necessary watchfulness which the other wants? Certainly not. Since the parable was designed to hold forth the prepared and the unprepared to meet Christ at His coming, and how the unprepared might, up to the very last, be confounded with the prepared--the structure of the parable behooved to accommodate itself to this, by making the lamps of the foolish to burn, as well as those of the wise, up to a certain point of time, and only then to discover their inability to burn on for want of a fresh supply of oil. But this is evidently just a structural device; and the real difference between the two classes who profess to love the Lord's appearing is a radical one--the possession by the one class of an enduring principle of spiritual life, and the want of it by the other. <div eID="gen26459" type="x-p"/>
entries.c6a2c81e06d57bb2cdf6aa6ea81b428ada36f96d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13791"/><div sID="gen26460" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13791"/><hi type="bold">8. And the foolish said unto the wise, Give us of your oil; for our lamps are gone out--</hi>rather, as in the Margin, "are going out"; for oil will not light an extinguished lamp, though it will keep a burning one from going out. Ah! now at length they have discovered not only their own folly, but the wisdom of the other class, and they do homage to it. They did not perhaps despise them before, but they thought them righteous overmuch; now they are forced, with bitter mortification, to wish they were like them. <div eID="gen26460" type="x-p"/>
entries.cf094fb4e718ffb754d28bbdca0b6a9e1bd9851c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13792"/><div sID="gen26461" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13792"/><hi type="bold">9. But the wise answered, Not so; lest there be not enough for us and you--</hi>The words "Not so," it will be seen, are not in the original, where the reply is very elliptical--"In case there be not enough for us and you." A truly wise answer this. "And what, then, if we shall share it with you? Why, both will be undone."<div eID="gen26461" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26462" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but go ye rather to them that sell, and buy for yourselves--</hi>Here again it would be straining the parable beyond its legitimate design to make it teach that men may get salvation even after they are supposed and required to have it already gotten. It is merely a friendly way of reminding them of the proper way of obtaining the needed and precious article, with a certain reflection on them for having it now to seek. Also, when the parable speaks of "selling" and "buying" that valuable article, it means simply, "Go, get it in the only legitimate way." And yet the word "buy" is significant; for we are elsewhere bidden, "buy wine and milk without money and without price," and "buy of Christ gold tried in the fire," &c. (<reference osisRef="Isa.55.1">Is 55:1</reference>; <reference osisRef="Rev.3.18">Re 3:18</reference>). Now, since what we pay the demanded price for becomes thereby our own property, the salvation which we thus take gratuitously at God's hands, being bought in His own sense of that word, becomes ours thereby in inalienable possession. (Compare for the language, <reference osisRef="Prov.23.23">Pr 23:23</reference>; <reference osisRef="Matt.13.44">Mt 13:44</reference>). <div eID="gen26462" type="x-p"/>
entries.4fb820f28bc363a198c1593e24717e4ec6e10dd5: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13793"/><div sID="gen26463" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13793"/><hi type="bold">10. And while they went to buy, the Bridegroom came; and they that were ready went in with him to the marriage: and the door was shut--</hi>They are sensible of their past folly; they have taken good advice: they are in the act of getting what alone they lacked: a very little more, and they also are ready. But the Bridegroom comes; the ready are admitted; "the door is shut," and they are undone. How graphic and appalling this picture of one almost saved--but lost! <div eID="gen26463" type="x-p"/>
entries.77334b5d142b2623c5fcca3f3a3c581e0d02b1a7: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13794"/><div sID="gen26464" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13794"/><hi type="bold">11. Afterward came also the other virgins, saying, Lord, Lord, open to us--</hi>In <reference osisRef="Matt.7.22">Mt 7:22</reference> this reiteration of the name was an exclamation rather of surprise; here it is a piteous cry of urgency, bordering on despair. Ah! now at length their eyes are wide open, and they realize all the consequences of their past folly. <div eID="gen26464" type="x-p"/>
entries.3e9f41142c52ab92f03eeeb5433eea3bbc033224: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13795"/><div sID="gen26465" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13795"/><hi type="bold">12. But he answered and said, Verily I say unto you, I know you not--</hi>The attempt to establish a difference between "I know you not" here, and "I never knew you" in <reference osisRef="Matt.7.23">Mt 7:23</reference>--as if this were gentler, and so implied a milder fate, reserved for "the foolish" of this parable--is to be resisted, though advocated by such critics as Olshausen, Stier, and Alford. Besides being inconsistent with the general tenor of such language, and particularly the solemn moral of the whole (<reference osisRef="Matt.25.13">Mt 25:13</reference>), it is a kind of criticism which tampers with some of the most awful warnings regarding the future. If it be asked why unworthy guests were admitted to the marriage of the King's Son, in a former parable, and the foolish virgins are excluded in this one, we may answer, in the admirable words of Gerhard, quoted by Trench, that those festivities are celebrated in this life, in the Church militant; these at the last day, in the Church triumphant; to those, even they are admitted who are not adorned with the wedding garment; but to these, only they to whom it is granted to be arrayed in fine linen clean and white, which is the righteousness of saints (<reference osisRef="Rev.19.8">Re 19:8</reference>); to those, men are called by the trumpet of the Gospel; to these by the trumpet of the Archangel; to those, who enters may go out from them, or be cast out; who is once introduced to these never goes out, nor is cast out, from them any more: wherefore it is said, "The door is shut." <div eID="gen26465" type="x-p"/>
entries.bd1277a694b21d051fa1eab857e1fc0bb148d2d9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13796"/><div sID="gen26466" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13796"/><hi type="bold">13. Watch therefore; for ye know neither the day nor the hour wherein the Son of man cometh--</hi>This, the moral or practical lesson of the whole parable, needs no comment.<div eID="gen26466" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.25.14-Matt.25.30">Mt 25:14-30</reference>. Parable of the Talents.</title> <div sID="gen26467" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">This parable, while closely resembling it, is yet a different one from that of The Pounds, in <reference osisRef="Luke.19.11-Luke.19.27">Lu 19:11-27</reference>; though Calvin, Olshausen, Meyer, and others identify them--</hi>but not De Wette and Neander. For the difference between the two parables, see the opening remarks on that of The Pounds. While, as Trench observes with his usual felicity, "the virgins were represented as waiting for their Lord, we have the servants working for Him; there the inward spiritual life of the faithful was described; here his external activity. It is not, therefore, without good reason that they appear in their actual order--that of the Virgins first, and of the Talents following--since it is the sole condition of a profitable outward activity for the kingdom of God, that the life of God be diligently maintained within the heart." <div eID="gen26467" type="x-p"/>
entries.b087eb3a9589e3d354a1fa1afd6a46a13405c329: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13797"/><div sID="gen26468" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13797"/><hi type="bold">14. For the kingdom of heaven is as a man--</hi>The ellipsis is better supplied by our translators in the corresponding passage of Mark (<reference osisRef="Mark.13.34">Mr 13:34</reference>), "[For the Son of man is] as a man," &c.,<div eID="gen26468" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26469" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">travelling into a far country--</hi>or more simply, "going abroad." The idea of long "tarrying" is certainly implied here, since it is expressed in <reference osisRef="Matt.25.19">Mt 25:19</reference>.<div eID="gen26469" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26470" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">who called his own servants, and delivered unto them his goods--</hi>Between master and slaves this was not uncommon in ancient times. Christ's "servants" here mean all who, by their Christian profession, stand in the relation to Him of entire subjection. His "goods" mean all their gifts and endowments, whether original or acquired, natural or spiritual. As all that slaves have belongs to their master, so Christ has a claim to everything which belongs to His people, everything which, may be turned to good, and He demands its appropriation to His service, or, viewing it otherwise, they first offer it up to Him; as being "not their own, but bought with a price" (<reference osisRef="1Cor.6.19">1Co 6:19</reference>, <reference osisRef="1Cor.6.20">20</reference>), and He "delivers it to them" again to be put to use in His service. <div eID="gen26470" type="x-p"/>
entries.a26a3a56b673f8ebde211cf992dd8b1e5f04abc8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13798"/><div sID="gen26471" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13798"/><hi type="bold">15. And unto one he gave five talents, to another two, and to another one--</hi>While the proportion of gifts is different in each, the same fidelity is required of all, and equally rewarded. And thus there is perfect equity.<div eID="gen26471" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26472" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">to every man according to his several ability--</hi>his natural capacity as enlisted in Christ's service, and his opportunities in providence for employing the gifts bestowed on him.<div eID="gen26472" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26473" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and straightway took his journey--</hi>Compare <reference osisRef="Matt.21.33">Mt 21:33</reference>, where the same departure is ascribed to God, after setting up the ancient economy. In both cases, it denotes the leaving of men to the action of all those spiritual laws and influences of Heaven under which they have been graciously placed for their own salvation and the advancement of their Lord's kingdom. <div eID="gen26473" type="x-p"/>
entries.275429325bd9795f9a0675235e32e1190f0fb600: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13799"/><div sID="gen26474" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13799"/><hi type="bold">16. Then he that had received the five talents went and traded with the same--</hi>expressive of the activity which he put forth and the labor he bestowed.<div eID="gen26474" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26475" type="x-p"/> and made them other five talents. <div eID="gen26475" type="x-p"/>
entries.b3c3bb3e2808d0955e6ef3094b0cd472339d7e26: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13800"/><div sID="gen26476" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13800"/><hi type="bold">17. And likewise he that had received two he also gained other two--</hi>each doubling what he received, and therefore both equally faithful. <div eID="gen26476" type="x-p"/>
entries.9059d4982624b3dba8559a4e659dd18bd0475d3d: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13801"/><div sID="gen26477" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13801"/><hi type="bold">18. But he that had received one went and digged in the earth, and hid his lord's money--</hi>not misspending, but simply making no use of it. Nay, his action seems that of one anxious that the gift should not be misused or lost, but ready to be returned, just as he got it. <div eID="gen26477" type="x-p"/>
entries.daacff715459f3442b3d29fc64145e513cbd15aa: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13802"/><div sID="gen26478" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13802"/><hi type="bold">19. After a long time the lord of those servants cometh and reckoneth with them--</hi>That any one--within the lifetime of the apostles at least--with such words before them, should think that Jesus had given any reason to expect His Second Appearing within that period, would seem strange, did we not know the tendency of enthusiastic, ill-regulated love of His appearing ever to take this turn. <div eID="gen26478" type="x-p"/>
entries.080bf52bdd281608645545b25a1dceaa3994eaf0: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13803"/><div sID="gen26479" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13803"/><hi type="bold">20. Lord, thou deliveredst unto me five talents; behold, I have gained besides them five talents more--</hi>How beautifully does this illustrate what the beloved disciple says of "boldness in the day of judgment," and his desire that "when He shall appear we may have confidence, and not be ashamed before Him at His coming!" (<reference osisRef="1John.4.17">1Jo 4:17</reference>; 2:28). <div eID="gen26479" type="x-p"/>
entries.1557bdc3fb920aa2d33fb87460bff871c8a66e9a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13804"/><div sID="gen26480" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13804"/><hi type="bold">21. His lord said unto him, Well done--</hi>a single word, not of bare satisfaction, but of warm and delighted commendation. And from what Lips!<div eID="gen26480" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26481" type="x-p"/> thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things, &c. <div eID="gen26481" type="x-p"/>
entries.453015e3b7ec2230c8fec9540cf30a7b9d348b28: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13805"/><div sID="gen26482" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13805"/><hi type="bold">22. He also that had received two talents came ... good and faithful servant: thou hast been faithful over a few things, I will make thee ruler over many things--</hi>Both are commended in the same terms, and the reward of both is precisely the same. (See on <reference osisRef="Matt.25.15">Mt 25:15</reference>). Observe also the contrasts: "Thou hast been faithful as a servant; now be a ruler--thou hast been entrusted with a few things; now have dominion over many things."<div eID="gen26482" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26483" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">enter thou into the joy of thy lord--</hi>thy Lord's own joy. (See <reference osisRef="John.15.11">Joh 15:11</reference>; <reference osisRef="Heb.12.2">He 12:2</reference>). <div eID="gen26483" type="x-p"/>
entries.0ba86739363e9117e914c32a837d029656203975: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13806"/><div sID="gen26484" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13806"/>24. Then he which had received the one talent came and said, Lord, I <hi type="bold">knew thee that thou art an hard man--</hi>harsh. The word in Luke (<reference osisRef="Luke.19.21">Lu 19:21</reference>) is "austere."<div eID="gen26484" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26485" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">reaping where thou hast not sown, and gathering where thou hast not strawed--</hi>The sense is obvious: "I knew thou wast one whom it was impossible to serve, one whom nothing would please: exacting what was impracticable, and dissatisfied with what was attainable." Thus do men secretly think of God as a hard Master, and virtually throw on Him the blame of their fruitlessness. <div eID="gen26485" type="x-p"/>
entries.f1d7ad7b64973d56c3be8446b25788cd92acb0a8: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13807"/><div sID="gen26486" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13807"/><hi type="bold">25. And I was afraid--</hi>of making matters worse by meddling with it at all.<div eID="gen26486" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26487" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and went and hid thy talent in the earth--</hi>This depicts the conduct of all those who shut up their gifts from the active service of Christ, without actually prostituting them to unworthy uses. Fitly, therefore, may it, at least, comprehend those, to whom Trench refers, who, in the early Church, pleaded that they had enough to do with their own souls, and were afraid of losing them in trying to save others; and so, instead of being the salt of the earth, thought rather of keeping their own saltness by withdrawing sometimes into caves and wildernesses, from all those active ministries of love by which they might have served their brethren.<div eID="gen26487" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26488" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Thou wicked and slothful servant--</hi>"Wicked" or "bad" means "falsehearted," as opposed to the others, who are emphatically styled "good servants." The addition of "slothful" is to mark the precise nature of his wickedness: it consisted, it seems, not in his doing anything against, but simply nothing for his master.<div eID="gen26488" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26489" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">Thou knewest that I reap where I sowed not, and gather where I have not strawed--</hi>He takes the servant's own account of his demands, as expressing graphically enough, not the hardness which he had basely imputed to him, but simply his demand of a profitable return for the gift entrusted. <div eID="gen26489" type="x-p"/>
entries.951caddce1478dbe87444b2a7b94fb523e62e5f4: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13808"/><div sID="gen26490" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13808"/><hi type="bold">27. thou oughtest therefore to have put my money to the exchangers--</hi>the bankers.<div eID="gen26490" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26491" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and then at my coming I should have received mine own with usury--</hi>interest. <div eID="gen26491" type="x-p"/>
entries.e4b2da62568206f3ff1c5ca745123e2411e1e209: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13809"/><div sID="gen26492" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13809"/><hi type="bold">29. For unto every one that hath shall be given, &c.--</hi>See on <reference osisRef="Matt.13.12">Mt 13:12</reference>. <div eID="gen26492" type="x-p"/>
entries.486a0946cdb3b602917bd86e69d74c75eaeb2326: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13810"/><div sID="gen26493" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13810"/><hi type="bold">30. And cast ye--</hi>cast ye out.<div eID="gen26493" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26494" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">the unprofitable servant--</hi>the useless servant, that does his Master no service.<div eID="gen26494" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26495" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">into outer darkness--</hi>the darkness which is outside. On this expression see on <reference osisRef="Matt.22.13">Mt 22:13</reference>.<div eID="gen26495" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26496" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">there shall be weeping and gnashing of teeth--</hi>See on <reference osisRef="Matt.13.42">Mt 13:42</reference>.<div eID="gen26496" type="x-p"/> <title type="x-s3"><reference osisRef="Matt.25.31-Matt.25.46">Mt 25:31-46</reference>. The Last Judgment.</title> <div sID="gen26497" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">The close connection between this sublime scene--</hi>peculiar to Matthew--and the two preceding parables is too obvious to need pointing out. <div eID="gen26497" type="x-p"/>
entries.582780df26fc116984bd087b0408cf18c0336ff9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13811"/><div sID="gen26498" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13811"/><hi type="bold">31. When the Son of man shall come in his glory--</hi>His personal glory.<div eID="gen26498" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26499" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and all the holy angels with him--</hi>See <reference osisRef="Deut.33.2">De 33:2</reference>; <reference osisRef="Dan.7.9">Da 7:9</reference>, <reference osisRef="Dan.7.10">10</reference>; Jude 14; with <reference osisRef="Heb.1.6">He 1:6</reference>; <reference osisRef="1Pet.3.22">1Pe 3:22</reference>.<div eID="gen26499" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26500" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">then shall he sit upon the throne of his glory--</hi>the glory of His judicial authority. <div eID="gen26500" type="x-p"/>
entries.73eab417a7ca442ff0098b0cdaee5d4b45de82bb: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13812"/><div sID="gen26501" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13812"/><hi type="bold">32. And before him shall be gathered all nations--</hi>or, "all the nations." That this should be understood to mean the heathen nations, or all except believers in Christ, will seem amazing to any simple reader. Yet this is the exposition of Olshausen, Stier, Keil, Alford (though latterly with some diffidence), and of a number, though not all, of those who hold that Christ will come the second time before the millennium, and that the saints will be caught up to meet Him in the air before His appearing. Their chief argument is, the impossibility of any that ever knew the Lord Jesus wondering, at the Judgment Day, that they should be thought to have done--or left undone--anything "unto Christ." To that we shall advert when we come to it. But here we may just say, that if this scene does not describe a personal, public, final judgment on men, according to the treatment they have given to Christ--and consequently men within the Christian pale--we shall have to consider again whether our Lord's teaching on the greatest themes of human interest does indeed possess that incomparable simplicity and transparency of meaning which, by universal consent, has been ascribed to it. If it be said, But how can this be the general judgment, if only those within the Christian pale be embraced by it?--we answer, What is here described, as it certainly does not meet the case of all the family of Adam, is of course so far not general. But we have no right to conclude that the whole "judgment of the great day" will be limited to the point of view here presented. Other explanations will come up in the course of our exposition.<div eID="gen26501" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26502" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">and he shall separate them--</hi>now for the first time; the two classes having been mingled all along up to this awful moment.<div eID="gen26502" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26503" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">as a shepherd divideth his sheep from the goats--</hi>(See <reference osisRef="Ezek.34.17">Eze 34:17</reference>). <div eID="gen26503" type="x-p"/>
entries.d8e76d603a5b47da019df9de38ab5f4b3bb1af1a: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13813"/><div sID="gen26504" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13813"/><hi type="bold">33. And he shall set the sheep on his right hand--</hi>the side of honor (<reference osisRef="1Kgs.2.19">1Ki 2:19</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.45.9">Psa 45:9</reference>; <reference osisRef="Ps.110.1">110:1</reference>, &c.).<div eID="gen26504" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26505" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">but the goats on the left--</hi>the side consequently of dishonor. <div eID="gen26505" type="x-p"/>
entries.89f8a232a8567a06d29ae57e69afb57c0dac788c: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13814"/><div sID="gen26506" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13814"/><hi type="bold">34. Then shall the King--</hi>Magnificent title, here for the first and only time, save in parabolical language, given to Himself by the Lord Jesus, and that on the eve of His deepest humiliation! It is to intimate that in then addressing the heirs of the kingdom, He will put on all His regal majesty.<div eID="gen26506" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26507" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">say unto them on his right hand, Come--</hi>the same sweet word with which He had so long invited all the weary and heavy laden to come unto Him for rest. Now it is addressed exclusively to such as have come and found rest. It is still, "Come," and to "rest" too; but to rest in a higher style, and in another region.<div eID="gen26507" type="x-p"/> <div sID="gen26508" type="x-p"/><hi type="bold">ye blessed of my Father, inherit the kingdom prepared for you from the foundation of the world--</hi>The whole story of this their blessedness is given by the apostle, in words which seem but an expression of these: "Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who hath blessed us with all spiritual blessings in heavenly places in Christ; according as He hath chosen us in Him before the foundation of the world, that we should be holy and without blame before Him in love." They were chosen from everlasting to the possession and enjoyment of all spiritual blessings in Christ, and so chosen in order to be holy and blameless in love. This is the holy love whose practical manifestations the King is about to recount in detail; and thus we see that their whole life of love to Christ is the fruit of an eternal purpose of love to them in Christ. <div eID="gen26508" type="x-p"/>
entries.e41974a9fa3b0a4eee8821b1cf634e3500b91ebe: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13815"/><div sID="gen26509" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13815"/>35. For I was an hungered ... thirsty ... a stranger, &c. <div eID="gen26509" type="x-p"/>
entries.3055a126a07903aa5bee381cd6e41568081d861f: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13816"/><div sID="gen26510" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13816"/>36. Naked ... sick ... prison, and ye came unto me. <div eID="gen26510" type="x-p"/>
entries.03490f350dc158ff91749e8ba2b2ffab153df9c9: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13817"/><div sID="gen26511" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13817"/>37-39. Then shall the righteous answer him, &c. <div eID="gen26511" type="x-p"/>
entries.b6a63a0f37a7849f62b034ea925f33f9e4e499e6: <div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" sID="pv13818"/><div sID="gen26512" type="x-p"/><div type="x-milestone" subType="x-preverse" eID="pv13818"/><hi type="bold">40. And the King shall answer and say unto them, Verily I say unto you, &c.--</hi>Astonishing dialogue this between the King, from the Throne of His glory, and His wondering people! "I was an hungered, and ye gave Me meat," &c.--"Not we," they reply. "We never did that, Lord: We were born out of due time, and enjoyed not the privilege of ministering unto Thee." "But ye did it to these My brethren, now beside you, when cast upon your love." "Truth, Lord, but was that doing it to Thee?
